review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Rodents are widely used in immunology but do not always recapitulate human immune functions. The tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri) is phylogenetically closer to primates than rodents and may help bridge this gap, yet its immune system has not been comprehensively characterised at single-cell resolution. Here, we present a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the tree shrew immune system, profiling 39 cell types across 12 tissues. We uncover human-like tonsillar structures and two transcriptionally distinct splenic macrophage subsets: an NR1H3+ immunoregulatory subset and an IRF8+ pro-inflammatory subset. During acute Epstein-Barr virus infection, NR1H3+ macrophages undergo pronounced inflammatory reprogramming and emerge as a major intercellular signalling hub. Cross-species integration of single-cell datasets from seven vertebrate species indicates that NR1H3+ macrophage gene programs are evolutionarily conserved. Functional analyses further support a shared anti-inflammatory programme mediated by NR1H3-dependent suppression of the non-canonical NF-κB pathway in both tree shrew and human macrophages. Together, these findings provide a reference resource for tree shrew immunology and support the tree shrew as a complementary model alongside rodent and primate systems.

---

## Introduction

Animal models play indispensable roles in understanding human diseases and developing effective therapeutic interventions. Rodents are widely used because they are accessible and supported by well-established experimental tools, but they do not always recapitulate human physiology and pathology, raising concerns about translational studies1–3. For example, mice and rats are not naturally susceptible to hepatitis viruses4, herpesviruses5 or SARS-CoV-26, partly because they lack key entry receptors, which limits their utility for studying these infections.

Nonhuman primates (NHPs) can provide more translatable insights. For example, smaller New World NHPs such as cottontop tamarins and common marmosets have served as experimental systems for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) positive lymphoma models7. However, ethical, cost and availability constraints limit NHPs research, underscoring the need for alternative small-animal models that more closely mirror human biology8. One promising candidate is the tree shrew, a small mammal that combines the practical advantages of rodents (compact size, rapid reproduction, short lifespan, and cost-effectiveness) with a closer evolutionary affinity to primates9,10. Tree shrews share many physiological and molecular features with primates, including immune system components11,12, and are susceptible to several human pathogens that do not infect mice, such as hepatitis B/C/D viruses, EBV and Zika virus13–16. Genomic analyses further support their close phylogenetic relationship with primates17,18. Despite these advantages, the paucity of species-specific research tools (e.g., well-characterized antibodies) has hampered broader application of tree shrews, particularly in immunological studies that rely on defined cell markers19.

Advances in single-cell genomics now offer a way to surmount this limitation. High-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology enables comprehensive characterization of cell populations without the need for species-specific reagents20. This approach provides an opportunity to characterize nontraditional model organisms such as tree shrew at molecular resolution. Indeed, recent cross-species single-cell studies have uncovered immune cell subsets and gene regulatory programs, illustrating the value of this approach21–25.

Here we map the immune landscape of the tree shrew using single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing across 12 tissues. We identify 39 distinct cell types and reveal well-developed tonsillar structures analogous to human tonsils, which are absent in rodents. Moreover, we define two splenic macrophage states (NR1H3+ and IRF8+) with distinct inflammatory programs that shift during acute EBV infection. Cross-species integration and functional assays show that NR1H3+ macrophages and NR1H3-dependent suppression of non-canonical NF-κB signalling are conserved between tree shrew and human. Together, these findings provide a reference for tree shrew immunology and support its use as a complementary small-animal model for translational and comparative studies.

---

## Results

Construction of a multitissue single-cell atlas reveals the cellular diversity of tree shrew

To systematically characterize the cellular heterogeneity of the tree shrew, we constructed a high-resolution single-cell atlas using scRNA-seq (Fig. 1A). We generated 24 sc/snRNA‑seq libraries from 12 tissues from three adult tree shrews. Immune‑related tissues were sampled across animals, whereas non‑immune parenchymal tissues and the pharyngeal tonsil were profiled once because of scope and tissue availability (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Data 1). Most tissues were analysed via scRNA-seq, but single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was used for the heart and liver to mitigate dissociation-associated bias for large or fragile cells26. A total of 221,113 cells/nuclei were recovered and passed initial quality control, and 186,973 high-quality cells/nuclei were retained after downstream filtering and doublet removal. Cell numbers ranged from 2,765 in pharyngeal tonsil to 30,645 in lymph tissue (Fig. 1B). We integrated all of the scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq data using the reciprocal principal component analysis (RPCA) method to correct for potential batch effects27. Unsupervised clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) clearly delineated major cell types, including endothelial cells, fibroblasts, haematopoietic stem cells and multipotent progenitor cells (HSC/MPP), myeloid cells, parenchymal cells, platelets, B and T cells (Supplementary Fig. 1). Given cost considerations, we prioritised biological replication for immune tissues; most non-immune parenchymal tissues were profiled once. Nevertheless, cells from the same tissue (or functionally related immune tissues such as lymph nodes, spleen and palatine tonsils) showed consistent distributions across animals (Supplementary Fig. 2), supporting the robustness of our atlas. Moreover, profiling multiple tissues from the same individual allowed us to control for inter-individual variables such as age, sex, diet and environment.

Further high-resolution clustering based on the expression of marker genes identified 39 distinct cell clusters within eight major cell classes in the global UMAP of all tissues (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 3). On average, each cell expressed 1,985 genes and 6,641 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs). The number of cells varied across the 39 cell types, ranging from 128 proliferating T cells to 17,776 double-positive T cells (DP T) (Supplementary Fig. 4). As expected, parenchymal subclusters were largely tissue-restricted, whereas multiple immune cell types were shared across tissues (Supplementary Fig. 5). Tissue-preference analysis further indicated that each tissue has a distinct immune neighbourhood; for example, although spleen and lymph nodes were both enriched for B cells, their myeloid compositions differed (Fig. 1D).

To further validate atlas annotations and explore underlying regulatory programs, we performed a SCENIC analysis to reconstruct transcription factor regulons across cells/ tissues (Supplementary Fig. 6 and 7). Each module was driven by transcription factors whose activity was enriched in particular cell populations or tissues. These regulon modules showed expression patterns consistent with known cell-type distribution, and their target genes were enriched for functions characteristic of those cells or tissues. For instance, modules active in metabolically focused parenchymal cells were enriched for metabolic pathways, whereas those prominent in proliferative progenitors were enriched in cell-cycle processes. The analysis also highlighted key lineage-defining TFs (e.g. HNF1B in kidney cells28 and FOXM1/E2F-family in haematopoietic progenitors29), supporting the accuracy of our cell-type annotations (Supplementary Fig. 8 and 9). In an independent bone-marrow analysis, regulon-based clustering recapitulated the transcriptome-defined cell populations (Supplementary Fig. 10), further confirming the robustness of our cell identification. Overall, this integrative transcription factor network analysis confirmed that each identified cell type possesses a distinct and biologically coherent regulatory program.

Anatomical and functional validation of tonsillar immunity in tree shrew

To further investigate intratissue cellular heterogeneity, we focused on the tonsils, which lie at the intersection of the digestive respiratory tracts30. Unlike rodents, which rely on nasal-associated lymphoid tissue as the primary upper airway immune organ, tree shrews possess human-like tonsillar structures, offering a useful model for mucosal immunity31,32. Coronal head sections revealed two distinct lymphoid structures: palatine tonsils in the oropharyngeal mucosa and pharyngeal tonsils in the pharyngeal region (Fig. 2A). Single-cell sequencing of the palatine tonsils identified 17 distinct cell populations span immune and epithelial/stromal compartments, including B cells (CD79A/MS4A1; plasma cells MZB1/JCHAIN), CD4⁺ T‑cell states (naïve LEF1/SELL, memory S100A4/TNFRSF18, Treg FOXP3/LAG3, exhausted CTLA4/TOX), myeloid populations (macrophages CSF1R/CD68, dendritic cells FCER1A/ITGAX), and epithelial/secretory cells (EPCAM/KRT14/KRT16) (Fig. 2B, C). Pharyngeal tonsil cells were analysed separately (Supplementary Fig. 11). These markers are consistent with those reported for the corresponding human cell types33. For example, LEF is required for T-cell development, and FOXP3 is indispensable for regulatory T-cell suppressive function34,35. KEGG pathway analysis further revealed cell type-specific signatures. For example, the B- and T-cell receptor signalling pathways are enriched in B- and T-cell subtypes, respectively. Pathways such as the cytokine‒cytokine receptor interaction pathway, JAK‒STAT signalling pathway, and PI3K‒Akt signalling pathway were enriched in NK cells. Plasma cells were enriched for protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with their role in immunoglobulin production36 (Fig. 2D). We subsequently validated representative markers in palatine tonsils by immunohistochemistry. CD3D (T-lineage) was prominent in peripheral regions of germinal centres, whereas CD79A (B-lineage) showed strong staining within germinal centres (Fig. 2E). MKI67, which marks proliferating cells across active phases of the cell cycle37, was detected in basal epithelial cells and germinal-centre cells. BCL6 and CR2 were enriched in germinal-centre cells, consistent with findings from human tonsil scRNA-seq33. Finally, KRT14 marked epithelial cells.

In tree shrew pharyngeal tonsils, ciliated cells expressed TPPP3, NEK10, and EPCAM, whereas glandular cells expressed AQP5 and FAM3D. Goblet cells expressed KRT15 and VMO1. Immune cells, including B cells, T cells and macrophages, were also present (Supplementary Fig. 11A-D). KEGG enrichment analysis showed enrichment of B- and T-cell receptor signalling pathways in B and T cells, respectively. Ciliated cells were enriched for thiamine metabolism, consistent with high energy demand, whereas glandular cells were enriched for salivary secretion pathways38 (Supplementary Fig. 11E). Immunohistochemical staining confirmed canonical markers (CD3D, CD79A, MKI67, BCL6, CR2 and AQP5) in pharyngeal tonsil sections (Supplementary Fig. 11F). Although scRNA-seq recovered relatively few B cells and plasma cells and did not capture mature/activated B-cell subsets, immunohistochemistry revealed germinal centres, indicating that these populations are present in vivo and were likely under-sampled because of limited tissue yield.

Tissue-specific functional diversity of tree shrew macrophages

Following comprehensive characterization of baseline cellular diversity, we next investigated the tissue-specific adaptation of macrophages in tree shrew. Although tissue-resident macrophages are recognized as pivotal regulators of tissue homeostasis and inflammatory responses in mammals39,40, their functional specialization and transcriptional landscape remain unexplored in this emerging model organism. We extracted 10,466 high-quality cells previously annotated as macrophages from all 12 tissues. Expression of the conserved macrophage marker CSF1R confirmed their identity (Fig. 3A). Immunofluorescence staining in spleen tissue further validated CSF1R expression, with CSF1R+ macrophages anatomically localised at the periphery of BCL6+ germinal centres (Fig. 3B), consistent with expected localisation. Macrophages from stomach (n = 44), pharyngeal tonsil (n = 92) and kidney (n = 0) were excluded because of insufficient cell numbers for robust subpopulation analysis. After batch correction, unsupervised clustering revealed nine transcriptionally distinct macrophage subpopulations (Fig. 3C, Supplementary Data 2). Tissue preference analysis using observed-to-expected cell ratios (Ro/e)41 demonstrated striking tissue specificity, with each subcluster showing strong enrichment in particular tissues (Ro/e >5) (Fig. 3D). Functional annotation of subcluster-defining genes (top 50 markers) by Gene Ontology (GO) analysis provided evidence for tissue microenvironment-driven specialization (Fig. 3E). For example, hepatic macrophages (C2) were enriched in metabolic regulation pathways, including the urea cycle, nitrogen cycle metabolic process, and L-arginine transmembrane transport, consistent with liver detoxification functions. Cardiac macrophages (C3) showed signatures of cardiac muscle contraction, heart morphogenesis, and actin cytoskeleton organization, suggesting roles in myocardial maintenance. In contrast to macrophages from other tissues, spleen macrophages presented two transcriptionally divergent subclusters (C4, C7) that were strongly spleen-enriched (Ro/e > 5) yet displayed functional divergence beyond typical tissue-driven specialization (Fig. 3C, D). Consistent spatial distributions of the C4 and C7 subclusters across triplicate spleen samples in UMAP plots (Supplementary Fig. 12) suggested genuine heterogeneity rather than batch effects. C4 macrophages were characterized by elevated expression of NR1H3 and PPARG (anti-inflammatory markers), whereas C7 macrophages expressed high levels of FLT3, IRF8, and CD226 (proinflammatory markers) (Fig. 3E). GO analysis of C4-defining genes highlighted pathways related to immunosuppression (e.g., negative regulation of macrophage activation, complement activation, and negative regulation of the type II interferon response), whereas C7 markers were linked to leukocyte activation, cell killing, and positive regulation of type II interferon production (Fig. 3E).

NR1H3⁺ macrophages undergo reprogramming during acute EBV infection

To investigate how splenic macrophage subsets respond to inflammatory stress, we leveraged our tree shrew EBV infection model13 and analysed acute infection (3–7 days post-infection, dpi). We focused on the acute phase to minimisNe confounding effects from monocyte-derived macrophage infiltration that is typically observed during chronic infection42, thereby preserving our analytical focus on tissue-resident macrophage populations. After quality control, we obtained 70,200 high-quality splenic scRNA-seq profiles (control: 17,372; 3 dpi: 28,590; 7 dpi: 24,238) that clustered into 10 populations after batch correction (Fig. 4A, B). UMAP visualization revealed a conserved cellular architecture without infection-induced clusters (Supplementary Fig. 13A), enabling direct comparison of preidentified macrophage subsets. A brief T/NKT analysis is provided in Supplementary Fig. 14. CellChat analysis showed that the number of inferred interactions was conserved across groups, whereas overall communication strength increased during acute infection, consistent with intensified intercellular signalling (Fig. 4C). Subcluster-specific communication strength analysis revealed NR1H3_Macro as a major signalling hub and cytokine source, with sharply increased incoming and outgoing interaction strength at 3 dpi (Fig. 4D). By contrast, IRF8_Macro showed reduced communication strength (Fig. 4D). Pathway analysis indicated activation of IFNG signalling (Supplementary Fig. 13B), with IFNG_NKT cells acting as senders and NR1H3_Macro as receivers via IFNGR1/2 (Supplementary Fig. 13D). NR1H3_Macro also transitioned towards a TNF-secreting phenotype and emerged as a key sender through TNF–TNFRSF1B interactions (Supplementary Fig. 13C). Although the abundance of NR1H3_Macro and IRF8_Macro remained stable across infection stages (Fig. 4E, F), their transcriptional states diverged. UCell scoring using subset-specific markers showed attenuation of anti-inflammatory signatures in NR1H3_Macro, whereas IRF8_Macro scores unchanged (Fig. 4G). Consistently, differential expression analysis within NR1H3_Macro revealed infection-induced downregulation of NR1H3 together with upregulation of proinflammatory mediators (IL1B, TNF, TNFSF9 and TNFSF14) and complement components (C1QA, C1QB and C1QC) (Fig. 4H, I). These results suggest that NR1H3 acts as a rheostat that constrains macrophage inflammatory potential, and its suppression permits inflammatory activation.

Conservation of NR1H3-mediated immunosuppression in human macrophages

Given the prominence of NR1H3⁺ macrophages in tree shrew, we asked whether a similar population exists in humans and exhibits conserved functions. NR1H3+ macrophages have been identified in human spleen scRNA-seq datasets43, and their expression profiles correlated with those of tree shrew (r=0.769, p < 0.01) (Fig. 5A, B, Supplementary Fig. 15), supporting conserved functions. To test function, we generated human NR1H3-overexpressing (NR1H3-OE) and NR1H3-knockdown (NR1H3-KO) THP-1 cell lines using lentivirus transduction system (Fig. 5C). Both NR1H3-OE and NR1H3-KO THP-1 cells differentiated normally, indicating that NR1H3 gain or NR1H3 loss of function did not grossly alter THP-1 macrophage differentiation (Fig. 5D). In functional assays, NR1H3 gain in THP‑1 macrophages reduced secretion of IL‑1β, IL‑6 and TNF‑α, modestly decreased uptake of bacterial particles, and diminished IFN‑γ production and effector polarization of primary CD8⁺ T cells while leaving T‑cell proliferation unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 17A–F). Furthermore, pharmacologic activation of NR1H3 with T0901317 in primary human monocyte‑derived macrophages similarly suppressed LPS‑induced IL‑1β, TNF‑α and IL‑6 release (Supplementary Fig. 17G, H), underscoring the translational relevance of NR1H3‑mediated immunoregulation.

We next performed bulk RNA-seq on NR1H3-OE and wild-type (WT) cells. Consistent with findings in the tree shrew model, TNF (log FoldChange = -1.73, p < 0.01), TNFSF14 (log FoldChange = -0.88, p < 0.01), and C1QA (log FoldChange = -1.37, p = 0.04) were downregulated in NR1H3-OE macrophages (Fig. 5E and Supplementary Data 3). Furthermore, key non-canonical NF-κB pathway-associated genes, including NFKBIZ (log FoldChange = -0.77, p = 0.02), NFKB2 (log FoldChange = -1.29, p < 0.01), and MAP3K14 (log FoldChange = -1.36, p < 0.01), were also repressed (Fig. 5E). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the Reactome database showed negative enrichment of REACTOME_TNF_RECEPTOR_SUPERFAMILY_TNFSF_MEMBERS_MEDIATING_NON_CANONICAL_NF_KB_PATHWAY in NR1H3-OE macrophages (NES=-1.49, p = 0.047) (Fig. 5F and Supplementary Data 4). Altered expression of selected genes was validated by qRT–PCR (Fig. 5G). To test whether NR1H3 directly binds to these loci, we performed NR1H3 cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis (Fig. 5H and Supplementary Data 5). At NR1H3-OE-induced gene loci, NR1H3 binding was detected upstream of TNFSF14, NFKB2 and NFKBIZ (Fig. 5I). We further evaluated pharmacological activation using two NR1H3 agonists (T0901317 and GW3965) 44,45. These agonists increased NR1H3 protein abundance in THP-1 macrophages (Fig. 5J). Consistent with NR1H3-mediated repression, agonist-dependent suppression of TNFSF14, NFKB2 and NFKBIZ was attenuated in NR1H3-KO THP-1 macrophages (Fig. 5K), supporting an NR1H3-dependent mechanism.

Cross-species integration highlights tree shrew as a phylogenetic bridge

Given the conserved role of NR1H3 in human and tree shrew macrophages, we investigated whether the identified regulatory mechanism represents a broader feature preserved across vertebrate evolution. To minimise confounding effects of tissue microenvironment-driven specialization, we focused on splenic macrophages. We integrated publicly available spleen scRNA-seq data across seven vertebrate species (GEO accession GSE186158), including primates (human and macaque), a close relative of primates (tree shrew), and commonly used experimental models spanning diverse lineages (pigs, rats, mice, and zebrafish). After quality control, the integrated map consisted of 88,106 cells (approximately 10,000 cells for each species), and was annotated into four major immune lineages based on canonical markers (Fig. 6A-B, Supplementary Fig. 18A). To compare cross‑species macrophage programs, we generated pseudobulk profiles by aggregating splenic macrophages within each species to reduce technical noise, and performed multidimensional scaling (MDS) on these profiles. The MDS projection broadly reflected phylogenetic relationships and positioned tree shrew between rodents and primates (Fig. 6C).

We first identified a core set of conserved macrophage genes broadly expressed across species, including CSF1R, NR1H3, CFP, CTSB, PSAP, LGMN, and ASAH1. CSF1R showed consistent expression across all species (Fig. 6D and E). NR1H3 expression varied across datasets, with low expression in mouse macrophages compared with higher expression in human and tree shrew macrophages (Fig. 6E). We next examined conservation of functional macrophage programs. Cytokine-related gene sets (IL1B, IL4R, IL10RA, TGFB1, IFNAR1, IFNGR1, TNFAIP8, TNFRSF14, and TNFRSF1B) were broadly conserved across species, with zebrafish showing a reduced set (TNFRSF14 and TGFB1). Chemokine gene (CCL4, CCL5, CXCR4, CXCL10, and CXCL16) showed closer similarity between tree shrew and human than between macaque and human in this dataset, differing mainly at CCL5. Complement-related genes (C1QA, C1QB, C1QBP, and C1QC) were largely conserved (Fig. 6E). To further explore the species-specific transcriptional features, we applied high-dimensional weighted gene coexpression network analysis (hdWGCNA)47 and identified 23 modules (Supplementary Fig. 18 B, C, Supplementary Data 6). We computed Pearson correlations between module genes and species labels, and designated the module with the highest correlation coefficient as the signature module for each species (Fig. 6F). Species-specific module genes were subjected to GO enrichment analysis using topGO (v2.38.1) (Fig. 6G and Supplementary Fig. 18 D). Although each species exhibited distinct functional characteristics associated with its macrophage-specific modules, many enriched terms converged on immune development and inflammatory pathways. Together, these results highlight both conservation and divergence of splenic macrophage programmes across vertebrates and support the tree shrew as a phylogenetically intermediate model for studying human-relevant immunological mechanisms.

---

## Methods

Ethics statement

For the multi-organ single-cell atlas, tissues were collected from three adult tree shrews (two males and one female; 8 months old; 120.5 ± 4.3 g). For the EBV infection experiments, twelve tree shrews (8 months old; 123.1 ± 7.6 g) were randomly assigned to the 3 dpi and 7 dpi groups (n = 6 per group; three males and three females per group), and tissues were collected at the indicated time points. All tree shrews were housed separately in a semi-barrier facility at 23°C–25°C and 40%–50% humidity under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle, with ad libitum access to standard chow and water60. All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Ethics Review Committee of Guangxi Medical University (approval no. 202101025) and were conducted in accordance with the Guiding Principles for the Use and Care of Experimental Animals issued by the Ministry of Science and Technology of China. Animals were euthanized by overdose of sodium pentobarbital followed by cervical dislocation prior to tissue collection.

Human peripheral blood samples were obtained from three healthy adult volunteers (two males and one female; 23-25 years old) for PBMC isolation. All participants provided written informed consent, and all uses of human material were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (approval no. 2025-E0760). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant local regulations.

Tissue dissociation and sample preparation for single-nucleus/cell library generation

Tissues were collected from 12 different samples: the spleen, thymus, tonsil, lymph nodes, nasopharynx, marrow, PBMCs, lung, liver, heart, kidney and stomach. Parenchymal tissues (except liver and heart) were placed in prechilled Hanks’ balanced salt solution (HBSS, Thermo Fisher Scientific) immediately after dissection. Samples were sliced into 3-4 mm3 pieces and digested into a cell suspension using digestion buffer containing 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Sigma‒Aldrich) and 1 mg/mL collagenase II (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were passed through a 70 μm strainer to remove the undigested tissue and centrifuged at 300 ×g for 5 min at 4 °C. Pelleted cells were resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (Solarbio) and incubated for 1 min at 4 °C. After washing twice with DPBS (Gibco), cell pellets were resuspended in sorting buffer (DPBS supplemented with 1% FBS). To mitigate dissociation-associated bias for large or fragile cells61, snRNA-seq was performed on liver and heart. Single-cell suspensions were captured in 10 × Genomics Chromium Single-Cell 5’ Solution, and single nuclei were captured in 10 × Genomics Chromium Single-cell 3’ Solution. The scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq library was generated by Beijing Novogene Company and prepared following the manufacturer’s protocol.

Raw data processing

Raw reads were aligned to the tree shrew reference genome (TupChi_1.0; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000334495.1/) using the Cell Ranger v6.1.0 pipeline (10 × Genomics) with default parameters, followed by barcode assignment and unique molecular identifier (UMI) counting. Filtered count matrices were imported into Seurat (v4.0.0)62 for downstream processing. Potential doublets were detected and filtered using DoubletFinder63 with default parameters. The cells/nuclei were filtered on the basis of a minimal expression threshold of 500 genes and 1000 UMIs, as well as genes that were expressed in at least five cells/nuclei. To remove outliers, we discarded cells in the bottom 1% and top 1% of the gene and UMI distributions per library, and removed cells/nuclei with more than 30% mitochondrial counts. Filtered data were normalized with Seurat’s NormalizeData function and highly variable features (n = 2000) were selected using the “vst” method. Datasets across organs and modalities (scRNA‑seq/snRNA‑seq) were integrated using Seurat’s RPCA anchor‑based workflow. We computed 20 principal components (“RunPCA”) to mitigate batch effects, and generated a UMAP embedding for visualization. Clustering was performed using shared nearest neighbour graph clustering (Louvain community detection-based method) with “FindClusters” at resolution of 1.2. Cell types were annotated in two stages. First, major cell classes (immune, endothelial, epithelial, fibroblast, and parenchymal compartments) were assigned using canonical markers and cluster-defining genes identified with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (default parameters). Second, immune‑cell subtypes were assigned using CellTypist (model: “Immune_All_High.pkl”; default settings) after mapping tree shrew genes to their human orthologs. Final labels were derived by a cluster‑level majority‑voting rule subject to a pre‑specified label‑probability threshold; cells not meeting this threshold were retained as “unassigned” and subsequently curated using canonical markers. Non‑immune subtypes were annotated using curated tissue‑specific marker panels from the literature and cross‑validated against the “FindAllMarkers”. Representative marker profiles for the 39 annotated cell types are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Gene regulatory network construction

A list of tree shrew transcription factors was downloaded from AnimalTFDB3.064. We applied SCENIC (v0.10.0) to infer regulatory networks. TF-target pairs with weight values greater than 0.01 were retained to define coexpression modules. AUCell scores were computed to quantify regulon activity in each cell. The final cell type- and tissue-specific gene regulatory networks were visualized in Cytoscape 3.7.2 (https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape).

Cell–cell interaction analysis

Interactions among different cell types were predicted with the CellChat package (v1.1.3) based on curated ligand‒receptor pairs. Tree shrew genes were mapped to human orthologues (reciprocal best-hit BLASTP; Supplementary Data 7) to enable use of the human database. CellChatDB.human was used as the interaction database. The communication probabilities were calculated with the “computeCommunProb”, enriched ligand–receptor pairs were extracted using “extractEnrichedLR”. In addition, global communication patterns and signal networks were analysed using the built-in nonnegative matrix factorisation framework. Interactions with P value < 0.05 were considered significance.

Cross‑species comparisons

Public single-cell datasets for human, macaque, pigs, rats, mice, and zebrafish were obtained from the GEO database (accession number GSE186158) and processed using the same QC and normalization strategy prior to integration. For cross‑species analysis we restricted integration to spleen to minimize tissue‑driven heterogeneity and maintain consistency with the rest of the study. Orthologs were defined by reciprocal best‑hit BLAST of translated peptides against the human proteome; only one‑to‑one orthologs shared by all species were retained and gene identifiers were harmonized to human symbols (Supplementary Data 7). For each species, count matrices were processed in Seurat with SCTransform normalization, then performed integration using Seurat’s canonical correlation analysis (CCA) with default parameters. For between‑species transcriptomic similarity, we computed per‑species macrophage pseudobulk profiles, calculated Euclidean distances, and applied classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) to obtain the first two dimensions shown in the MDS plot46.

Statistical analysis

Data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise stated. Two-sided statistical tests were used throughout unless indicated. For two group comparisons, unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used for approximately normally distributed data; otherwise the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (or Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s test for non-parametric data) was applied. Where multiple hypotheses were tested (e.g., differential expression, enrichment analyses), P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and FDR < 0.05 was considered significant unless stated otherwise.

Data availability

The scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq and Cut&Tag data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1051046 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1051046). Human splenic scRNA-seq was obtained from the Tissue Immune Cell Atlas portal (https://www.tissueimmunecellatlas.org/#datasets). Public datasets used for cross-species analyses were obtained from GEO (accession GSE186158). Source data are provided with this paper. Primer sequences and antibodies used in this study are provided in Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Table 2, respectively.

Code availability

The custom code used in this study is available at https://github.com/xialabtools/Tree_shrew_scRNA_code. This repository has been archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17609696).

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript the authors analysed by single cell high-throughput RNA-seq several tissues from a small rodents (T.belangeri). The animal model was chosen because of a relatively higher similarity to humans with respect to mice and rats. Despite the inherently interesting findings regarding the tree shrew's immune system and its potential as a more representative model for human immunity, we have significant concerns regarding the reproducibility and the comprehensive functional validation of the study. The identification of human-like immune features, such as the tonsillar structure and the conserved NR1H3+ macrophage subset, is compelling, and the proposed role of these macrophages in EBV infection is particularly noteworthy.

However, few critical issues must be addressed to solidify the study’s impact.

General comments:
Insufficient Bioinformatics Pipeline Details and Reproducibility
Our primary concern lies with the insufficient description and accessibility of the bioinformatics pipeline. While the provided "Raw data processing" section offers a good start by detailing some steps, it lacks the comprehensive transparency needed for true reproducibility, especially for complex single-cell analyses. The paper outlines exciting discoveries, but without a complete understanding and direct access to the computational methods used, it's impossible for other researchers to independently verify or build upon these findings.

Specifically, while the authors have listed some software and parameters, they need to provide a far more thorough and transparent account of their bioinformatics approach. This includes, but is not limited to:
Custom Scripting and Workflows: The M&M section mentions specific packages and functions, but often single-cell analysis involves custom scripts to integrate these tools, perform specific filtering steps, or generate custom visualizations. These scripts, and the order in which they are executed, are crucial for replication.

Cell Type Annotation Strategy: A total of 39 cell types were identified in this paper, but the M&M section doesn't detail how these cell types were assigned. Was it based on known marker gene expression? Were external reference atlases used for annotation? This is a critical step that needs clear explanation.

Specifics of Cross-Species Comparison for CellChat: While it states "homologous gene mapping from T. belangeri to the human genome was first performed to identify the corresponding genes in humans," the method or tool used for this homologous mapping (e.g., BLAST, Ensembl Compara, custom ortholog tables) is missing. This is vital for the validity of the cross-species comparison in CellChat.

Version Control and Environment Management: Simply listing software versions is helpful, but the exact computational environment (e.g., operating system, specific R/Python versions, library dependencies) in which the analysis was performed is essential for ensuring that code runs without dependency conflicts or unexpected behavior.

Critically, to fully address the issue of reproducibility, I strongly recommend that the authors provide a link to a publicly accessible GitHub repository containing the complete analysis code. This repository should ideally be structured to allow for step-by-step execution of the analysis, from raw data processing to the generation of figures. Even better, the provision of a Docker container encapsulating the entire computational environment and analysis pipeline would be the gold standard.
This would allow any researcher to precisely replicate the computational steps and ensure the robustness of the reported findings, without encountering issues related to software installations or versioning.

2. Lack of Functional Validation for NR1H3 Activation
While the provided results presented in the paragraph “Conservation of NR1H3-mediated immunosuppression in human macrophages” demonstrate a strong correlation between NR1H3 activation and the downregulation of pro-inflammatory and non-canonical NF-KB pathway genes in THP-1 cells, it primarily focuses on transcriptional changes and direct binding. This is a valuable step, but it doesn't definitively prove the functional consequence of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression at a cellular or immunological level.

To demonstrate the "true functionality" of NR1H3 activation in immunosuppression, especially in the context of human macrophages, the following experiments would be helpful
a. Functional Assays on Macrophage Pro-inflammatory Responses:
Cytokine and chemokine Production Assays:
Measure secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines (using ELISA or multiplex cytokine arrays) upon stimulation with PAMPs/DAMPs from challenge NR1H3-OE, NR1H3-KO, and WT THP-1 cells
NR1H3 activation should lead to a reduction in these cytokines compared to WT or NR1H3-KO cells.
Phagocytosis Assay: While not directly linked to inflammation, some immunosuppressive macrophages might have altered phagocytic capabilities. This could be an exploratory experiment.

b. Immune cell crosstalk assays:
Co-culture Experiments with T cells (or other immune cells) can also give useful insight and functional readout. Therefore, a T cell Proliferation Assay can be performed to depict the biological consequences of NR1H3 activation. Likewise, the authors can investigate the T cell Cytokine Production and cell Differentiation

c. In Vivo Relevance/Translational Experiments (if feasible):
Ex vivo stimulation of human primary macrophages: If possible, obtain human primary macrophages (e.g., from PBMCs) and activate NR1H3 pharmacologically (with T0901317 or GW3965). Then, repeat the cytokine/chemokine production assays after inflammatory stimulation. This would bridge the gap from THP-1 cells to primary human
By incorporating these functional assays, the authors would move beyond solely demonstrating transcriptional changes and direct gene binding to definitively prove the "true functionality" of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression in human macrophages. This would significantly strengthen their claim about the conserved anti-inflammatory immunoregulatory function of NR1H3.

Specific comments:
1. The observed-to-expected cell ratios (Ro/e) presented in Fig 1 and Fig3D is not clear. What is the expected cell number? From which dataset does this derive? Wasn’t it worth to compare different tissues across themselves? As it is in this current version, the plot is not meaningful
2. Fig 5A/B. The human/T.belangeri macrophage similarity is unclear and not convincing. What exactly is represented in Fig 5B? What is each dot? It is indeed difficult to state the “similarity”similarity”” between two cell types in different organs, unless many cells are compared and the two in exams are more close to each other with respect to the distance between other cells.

Minor comments:
In the text, the experimental strategy is not clearly presented. The reader expects to have 36 samples, 12 tissues from three animals, but only 24 samples are actually there (3 for immune organs, one for other and one for pharyngeal tonsil). This must be better addressed at the beginning of the results.
The differences between gender is not analyzed in any of the main or supplementary figures. As there might be gender differences it is worth to analyze it and, especially for tissues where one single organ was processed, it is worth mentioning from which animal they were processed.
Fig 3e, the GO dot plot should be on the right of the GO terms, otherwise it seems the dots refers to the genes on the left
Line 102 the goal is not to alleviate the financial constraints, so “and” should be replaced with “while”
Line 158 fig 2e should be 2d
Line 159 2f should be 2e
Fig 2C unit metrics is missing from scale bar, the same applies to most figures (2D, 3A, 3E, 4B, 4F, 4H and so on)
The volcano plot legend of Fig5E is not clear. It is more common to highlight the significantly upregulated genes (top right) and the significantly downregulated ones (top left)
Supplementary figures are not mentioned in order in the text (i.e fig S11 comes after Fig S8)
In Fig6G human is misspelled
Fig 6C, this figure is not enough “per se” to state that T. belangeri is more close to humans than other species, as this plot might be dominated by strong species specific technical batch effect, rather than biological effect. Moreover, mice and rats seem to be closer to pigs than to themselves from this plot, which is counterintuitive and highlights possible misinterpretation or inadequate analysis.

### Reviewer 2

This study by Tang and colleagues presents a comprehensive single-cell immune cell atlas of Tupaia belangeri and provides compelling evidence that the tree shrew is a promising model organism for immunological research. By integrating multi-tissue profiling, EBV infection modeling, and cross-species comparisons, the authors effectively demonstrate the translational potential of Tupaia, particularly in contexts where conventional rodent models are limited.

Importance:
The study is meaningful in that it establishes a foundational resource for using Tupaia belangeri as a non-primate animal model. Its evolutionary proximity to humans and permissiveness to human-specific pathogens make it particularly valuable for translational studies, especially in the field of viral immunology.

Specific comments:
1. Data processing rigor:
Several aspects of data processing and integration require clearer explanation. For instance, how doublets were removed, what specific QC metrics were applied, and how batch effects were corrected are not sufficiently described. Given the inclusion of multiple tissues and time points, this methodological clarity is essential.
More specifically, the localization of T cells in Supplementary Fig. 1 appears questionable, suggesting that doublet removal may not have been adequately performed. Epithelial cell annotations also appear inconsistent across figures. I recommend the authors include UMAP plots annotated by major cell types (e.g., T cells, B cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts) to improve transparency.
Furthermore, batch correction and integration should be benchmarked using multiple methods (e.g., Harmony, scVI) rather than relying on a single approach.

2. Depth of analysis in the EBV model:
The EBV infection model is an important part of the study, but the analysis feels relatively shallow. For example, was EBV transcript detected in B cells or other cell types? Basic analyses such as pseudotime trajectory, cell type-specific differential gene expression (DEG), and pathway enrichment should be provided before diving into cell–cell communication analysis.
Additionally, recent tools like Milo could be combined with improved integration methods to track graph-level changes in cell proportions.

Minor comment: In Supplementary Fig. 13A, the temporal order should be displayed as Control → Day 3 → Day 7. Also, the terms “Pos-macro” and “Neg-macro” are not clearly defined and are inconsistent with previous labeling.

3. Cross-species comparison methodology:
The cross-species integration is one of the more exciting aspects of this paper, but its current implementation is too preliminary. Key technical steps—such as ortholog selection, normalization across species, and gene filtering—should be explained in more detail. Methods like SATURN or scGLUE could be applied here to improve both the interpretability and robustness of the analysis.
In particular, the MDS plot is difficult to interpret, and it is unclear what the axes represent. If this plot is intended to convey evolutionary distance or transcriptional similarity, it should be supplemented with more formal statistical support.
Additionally, the analysis of HLA loci, which are known to be highly divergent between species, needs to be handled with extra caution. Ortholog mapping for HLA genes should be genome-informed and well-documented.

### Reviewer 3

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 4

This new study describes a single cell immune atlas for the tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri). Tree shrews are an emerging small animal model that are evolutionarily closer to primates than mice. As such, tree shrews represent a useful, viable alternative model for infectious disease and aging studies that may be otherwise challenging to carryout in murine or non-human primate model systems. The investigators profiled single cells from 12 different tissues of 3 adult tree shrews, identifying 39 different cell types. Notably, bulk RNAseq studies have been performed in spleen, PBMCs, and other tissues from the tree shrew, and single cell transcriptome atlases have been recently published for brain and neurological tissues. A strength of this study is that it represents the first tree shrew immune-focused single cell atlas which can provide an important platform for understanding systemic transcriptional responses to infectious diseases in future studies. Aside from the substantial efforts that went into generating this resource, there are some key weaknesses and major concerns with the overall conclusions derived from the interpretation of the EBV infection data.

Major Concerns:
1. Atlas reveals that T.belangeri possess well-developed tonsillar structures analogous to human tonsils. These tonsillar anatomical structures within the oropharynx were previously reported for the tree shrew—and thus, it is expected that these tissues will harbor lymphoid cell types commonly observed in primate tonsils. However, in figure 1, mature and activated B cell subsets are not detected in the pharyngeal tonsils, which is unusual. Could this be due to sampling issues or issues with adequate sequencing coverage? As the tonsils are a significant focus of the paper (Fig 2), more work needs to be put into describing these cells. Fig. 2B needs to be described in detail—UMAP represents cells in which tonsils? There were only ~2700 cells sequenced for pharyngeal—were palantine and pharyngeal grouped together in this figure? Are the cell subsets and relative distributions of representative cell types in these tissues comparable to what is reported in human and nonhuman primate samples?

2. A major caveat is that the EBV infection model does not mimic natural oral uptake and natural viral transmission which is observed in other NHP models with LCVs (i.e. rhesus and cynomolgus macaque models). Here, the route of EBV administration is intravenous into the femoral vein, thus any relevance to palantine/pharyngeal tonsil responses—which the authors argue is an important component of the tree shrew model (Fig. 2)—is unclear as this requires trafficking of the virus to the oral/throat cavity (in previous publications with this tree shrew model, EBV shedding occurs at 7 dpi). It is unclear why tonsil cells were not sequenced from the infected animals as this would highlight the importance and biological relevance of these structures for EBV infection. The I.V. infection route and also the high titer virus administered is akin to what is utilized in mouse models, which does not recapitulate natural EBV infection in humans and this needs to be acknowledged. As such, the immune responses (i.e. bypassing mucosal immunity in the oral cavity and gut that occurs with oral challenge) are expected to be skewed.

3. The sample size for EBV experiments in Fig 4 is extremely small. Spleen cells are sequenced from only two animals that were infected with EBV and harvested at different time points, limiting the statistical power and generalizability of findings that NR1H3(LXRa+) macrophages are indeed altered by EBV infection. It is basically a pilot experiment. In an attempt to confirm scRNAseq findings, immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR experiments were performed on samples from 4 animals in Fig 4. No differences in NR1H3+ or IRF8+ macrophage numbers were detected by IFA, although the NR1H3 RNA level does decrease, which hardly confirms the scRNAseq findings. Given that data describing NR1H3 cell reprogramming is from n=1, additional evidence should be provided to support the major conclusions that NRH13+ macrophages dominate the inflammatory responses observed in EBV infection. For example, does depletion of these cells impact acute EBV infection? Are there additional signs of inflammatory markers that track with these macrophage subsets?

4. Depletion of liver X receptors (NR1H3 gene encodes LXRa) in mice leads to enhanced replication of a murine g-herpesvirus (MHV68) that is often used as a model for EBV infection (PMC6050960). Such prior studies indicate NRH13-mediated mechanisms are indeed conserved in mice.

5. The study largely focuses on describing B cells and macrophage subset, yet T cell responses are a major contributor to control of infectious agents that have been tested in tree shrew models (i.e. Zika, hepatitis virus). T cell populations should be described in detail.

Other minor comments:
1. Introduction, line 52: smaller NHPs such as marmosets and tamarins have been historically used for EBV infection studies and should be mentioned in this section.
2. Line 74, first single-cell atlas of T. belangeri and line 435: This is incorrectly stated as there are at least three other publications describing brain/neurological tissue-focused single cell atlases for the tree shrew.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Rodents are widely used in immunology but do not always recapitulate human immune functions. The tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri) is phylogenetically closer to primates than rodents and may help bridge this gap, yet its immune system has not been comprehensively characterised at single-cell resolution. Here, we present a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the tree shrew immune system, profiling 39 cell types across 12 tissues. We uncover human-like tonsillar structures and two transcriptionally distinct splenic macrophage subsets: an NR1H3+ immunoregulatory subset and an IRF8+ pro-inflammatory subset. During acute Epstein-Barr virus infection, NR1H3+ macrophages undergo pronounced inflammatory reprogramming and emerge as a major intercellular signalling hub. Cross-species integration of single-cell datasets from seven vertebrate species indicates that NR1H3+ macrophage gene programs are evolutionarily conserved. Functional analyses further support a shared anti-inflammatory programme mediated by NR1H3-dependent suppression of the non-canonical NF-κB pathway in both tree shrew and human macrophages. Together, these findings provide a reference resource for tree shrew immunology and support the tree shrew as a complementary model alongside rodent and primate systems.

---

## Introduction

Animal models play indispensable roles in understanding human diseases and developing effective therapeutic interventions. Rodents are widely used because they are accessible and supported by well-established experimental tools, but they do not always recapitulate human physiology and pathology, raising concerns about translational studies1–3. For example, mice and rats are not naturally susceptible to hepatitis viruses4, herpesviruses5 or SARS-CoV-26, partly because they lack key entry receptors, which limits their utility for studying these infections.

Nonhuman primates (NHPs) can provide more translatable insights. For example, smaller New World NHPs such as cottontop tamarins and common marmosets have served as experimental systems for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) positive lymphoma models7. However, ethical, cost and availability constraints limit NHPs research, underscoring the need for alternative small-animal models that more closely mirror human biology8. One promising candidate is the tree shrew, a small mammal that combines the practical advantages of rodents (compact size, rapid reproduction, short lifespan, and cost-effectiveness) with a closer evolutionary affinity to primates9,10. Tree shrews share many physiological and molecular features with primates, including immune system components11,12, and are susceptible to several human pathogens that do not infect mice, such as hepatitis B/C/D viruses, EBV and Zika virus13–16. Genomic analyses further support their close phylogenetic relationship with primates17,18. Despite these advantages, the paucity of species-specific research tools (e.g., well-characterized antibodies) has hampered broader application of tree shrews, particularly in immunological studies that rely on defined cell markers19.

Advances in single-cell genomics now offer a way to surmount this limitation. High-throughput single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology enables comprehensive characterization of cell populations without the need for species-specific reagents20. This approach provides an opportunity to characterize nontraditional model organisms such as tree shrew at molecular resolution. Indeed, recent cross-species single-cell studies have uncovered immune cell subsets and gene regulatory programs, illustrating the value of this approach21–25.

Here we map the immune landscape of the tree shrew using single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing across 12 tissues. We identify 39 distinct cell types and reveal well-developed tonsillar structures analogous to human tonsils, which are absent in rodents. Moreover, we define two splenic macrophage states (NR1H3+ and IRF8+) with distinct inflammatory programs that shift during acute EBV infection. Cross-species integration and functional assays show that NR1H3+ macrophages and NR1H3-dependent suppression of non-canonical NF-κB signalling are conserved between tree shrew and human. Together, these findings provide a reference for tree shrew immunology and support its use as a complementary small-animal model for translational and comparative studies.

---

## Results

Construction of a multitissue single-cell atlas reveals the cellular diversity of tree shrew

To systematically characterize the cellular heterogeneity of the tree shrew, we constructed a high-resolution single-cell atlas using scRNA-seq (Fig. 1A). We generated 24 sc/snRNA‑seq libraries from 12 tissues from three adult tree shrews. Immune‑related tissues were sampled across animals, whereas non‑immune parenchymal tissues and the pharyngeal tonsil were profiled once because of scope and tissue availability (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Data 1). Most tissues were analysed via scRNA-seq, but single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was used for the heart and liver to mitigate dissociation-associated bias for large or fragile cells26. A total of 221,113 cells/nuclei were recovered and passed initial quality control, and 186,973 high-quality cells/nuclei were retained after downstream filtering and doublet removal. Cell numbers ranged from 2,765 in pharyngeal tonsil to 30,645 in lymph tissue (Fig. 1B). We integrated all of the scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq data using the reciprocal principal component analysis (RPCA) method to correct for potential batch effects27. Unsupervised clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) clearly delineated major cell types, including endothelial cells, fibroblasts, haematopoietic stem cells and multipotent progenitor cells (HSC/MPP), myeloid cells, parenchymal cells, platelets, B and T cells (Supplementary Fig. 1). Given cost considerations, we prioritised biological replication for immune tissues; most non-immune parenchymal tissues were profiled once. Nevertheless, cells from the same tissue (or functionally related immune tissues such as lymph nodes, spleen and palatine tonsils) showed consistent distributions across animals (Supplementary Fig. 2), supporting the robustness of our atlas. Moreover, profiling multiple tissues from the same individual allowed us to control for inter-individual variables such as age, sex, diet and environment.

Further high-resolution clustering based on the expression of marker genes identified 39 distinct cell clusters within eight major cell classes in the global UMAP of all tissues (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 3). On average, each cell expressed 1,985 genes and 6,641 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs). The number of cells varied across the 39 cell types, ranging from 128 proliferating T cells to 17,776 double-positive T cells (DP T) (Supplementary Fig. 4). As expected, parenchymal subclusters were largely tissue-restricted, whereas multiple immune cell types were shared across tissues (Supplementary Fig. 5). Tissue-preference analysis further indicated that each tissue has a distinct immune neighbourhood; for example, although spleen and lymph nodes were both enriched for B cells, their myeloid compositions differed (Fig. 1D).

To further validate atlas annotations and explore underlying regulatory programs, we performed a SCENIC analysis to reconstruct transcription factor regulons across cells/ tissues (Supplementary Fig. 6 and 7). Each module was driven by transcription factors whose activity was enriched in particular cell populations or tissues. These regulon modules showed expression patterns consistent with known cell-type distribution, and their target genes were enriched for functions characteristic of those cells or tissues. For instance, modules active in metabolically focused parenchymal cells were enriched for metabolic pathways, whereas those prominent in proliferative progenitors were enriched in cell-cycle processes. The analysis also highlighted key lineage-defining TFs (e.g. HNF1B in kidney cells28 and FOXM1/E2F-family in haematopoietic progenitors29), supporting the accuracy of our cell-type annotations (Supplementary Fig. 8 and 9). In an independent bone-marrow analysis, regulon-based clustering recapitulated the transcriptome-defined cell populations (Supplementary Fig. 10), further confirming the robustness of our cell identification. Overall, this integrative transcription factor network analysis confirmed that each identified cell type possesses a distinct and biologically coherent regulatory program.

Anatomical and functional validation of tonsillar immunity in tree shrew

To further investigate intratissue cellular heterogeneity, we focused on the tonsils, which lie at the intersection of the digestive respiratory tracts30. Unlike rodents, which rely on nasal-associated lymphoid tissue as the primary upper airway immune organ, tree shrews possess human-like tonsillar structures, offering a useful model for mucosal immunity31,32. Coronal head sections revealed two distinct lymphoid structures: palatine tonsils in the oropharyngeal mucosa and pharyngeal tonsils in the pharyngeal region (Fig. 2A). Single-cell sequencing of the palatine tonsils identified 17 distinct cell populations span immune and epithelial/stromal compartments, including B cells (CD79A/MS4A1; plasma cells MZB1/JCHAIN), CD4⁺ T‑cell states (naïve LEF1/SELL, memory S100A4/TNFRSF18, Treg FOXP3/LAG3, exhausted CTLA4/TOX), myeloid populations (macrophages CSF1R/CD68, dendritic cells FCER1A/ITGAX), and epithelial/secretory cells (EPCAM/KRT14/KRT16) (Fig. 2B, C). Pharyngeal tonsil cells were analysed separately (Supplementary Fig. 11). These markers are consistent with those reported for the corresponding human cell types33. For example, LEF is required for T-cell development, and FOXP3 is indispensable for regulatory T-cell suppressive function34,35. KEGG pathway analysis further revealed cell type-specific signatures. For example, the B- and T-cell receptor signalling pathways are enriched in B- and T-cell subtypes, respectively. Pathways such as the cytokine‒cytokine receptor interaction pathway, JAK‒STAT signalling pathway, and PI3K‒Akt signalling pathway were enriched in NK cells. Plasma cells were enriched for protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with their role in immunoglobulin production36 (Fig. 2D). We subsequently validated representative markers in palatine tonsils by immunohistochemistry. CD3D (T-lineage) was prominent in peripheral regions of germinal centres, whereas CD79A (B-lineage) showed strong staining within germinal centres (Fig. 2E). MKI67, which marks proliferating cells across active phases of the cell cycle37, was detected in basal epithelial cells and germinal-centre cells. BCL6 and CR2 were enriched in germinal-centre cells, consistent with findings from human tonsil scRNA-seq33. Finally, KRT14 marked epithelial cells.

In tree shrew pharyngeal tonsils, ciliated cells expressed TPPP3, NEK10, and EPCAM, whereas glandular cells expressed AQP5 and FAM3D. Goblet cells expressed KRT15 and VMO1. Immune cells, including B cells, T cells and macrophages, were also present (Supplementary Fig. 11A-D). KEGG enrichment analysis showed enrichment of B- and T-cell receptor signalling pathways in B and T cells, respectively. Ciliated cells were enriched for thiamine metabolism, consistent with high energy demand, whereas glandular cells were enriched for salivary secretion pathways38 (Supplementary Fig. 11E). Immunohistochemical staining confirmed canonical markers (CD3D, CD79A, MKI67, BCL6, CR2 and AQP5) in pharyngeal tonsil sections (Supplementary Fig. 11F). Although scRNA-seq recovered relatively few B cells and plasma cells and did not capture mature/activated B-cell subsets, immunohistochemistry revealed germinal centres, indicating that these populations are present in vivo and were likely under-sampled because of limited tissue yield.

Tissue-specific functional diversity of tree shrew macrophages

Following comprehensive characterization of baseline cellular diversity, we next investigated the tissue-specific adaptation of macrophages in tree shrew. Although tissue-resident macrophages are recognized as pivotal regulators of tissue homeostasis and inflammatory responses in mammals39,40, their functional specialization and transcriptional landscape remain unexplored in this emerging model organism. We extracted 10,466 high-quality cells previously annotated as macrophages from all 12 tissues. Expression of the conserved macrophage marker CSF1R confirmed their identity (Fig. 3A). Immunofluorescence staining in spleen tissue further validated CSF1R expression, with CSF1R+ macrophages anatomically localised at the periphery of BCL6+ germinal centres (Fig. 3B), consistent with expected localisation. Macrophages from stomach (n = 44), pharyngeal tonsil (n = 92) and kidney (n = 0) were excluded because of insufficient cell numbers for robust subpopulation analysis. After batch correction, unsupervised clustering revealed nine transcriptionally distinct macrophage subpopulations (Fig. 3C, Supplementary Data 2). Tissue preference analysis using observed-to-expected cell ratios (Ro/e)41 demonstrated striking tissue specificity, with each subcluster showing strong enrichment in particular tissues (Ro/e >5) (Fig. 3D). Functional annotation of subcluster-defining genes (top 50 markers) by Gene Ontology (GO) analysis provided evidence for tissue microenvironment-driven specialization (Fig. 3E). For example, hepatic macrophages (C2) were enriched in metabolic regulation pathways, including the urea cycle, nitrogen cycle metabolic process, and L-arginine transmembrane transport, consistent with liver detoxification functions. Cardiac macrophages (C3) showed signatures of cardiac muscle contraction, heart morphogenesis, and actin cytoskeleton organization, suggesting roles in myocardial maintenance. In contrast to macrophages from other tissues, spleen macrophages presented two transcriptionally divergent subclusters (C4, C7) that were strongly spleen-enriched (Ro/e > 5) yet displayed functional divergence beyond typical tissue-driven specialization (Fig. 3C, D). Consistent spatial distributions of the C4 and C7 subclusters across triplicate spleen samples in UMAP plots (Supplementary Fig. 12) suggested genuine heterogeneity rather than batch effects. C4 macrophages were characterized by elevated expression of NR1H3 and PPARG (anti-inflammatory markers), whereas C7 macrophages expressed high levels of FLT3, IRF8, and CD226 (proinflammatory markers) (Fig. 3E). GO analysis of C4-defining genes highlighted pathways related to immunosuppression (e.g., negative regulation of macrophage activation, complement activation, and negative regulation of the type II interferon response), whereas C7 markers were linked to leukocyte activation, cell killing, and positive regulation of type II interferon production (Fig. 3E).

NR1H3⁺ macrophages undergo reprogramming during acute EBV infection

To investigate how splenic macrophage subsets respond to inflammatory stress, we leveraged our tree shrew EBV infection model13 and analysed acute infection (3–7 days post-infection, dpi). We focused on the acute phase to minimisNe confounding effects from monocyte-derived macrophage infiltration that is typically observed during chronic infection42, thereby preserving our analytical focus on tissue-resident macrophage populations. After quality control, we obtained 70,200 high-quality splenic scRNA-seq profiles (control: 17,372; 3 dpi: 28,590; 7 dpi: 24,238) that clustered into 10 populations after batch correction (Fig. 4A, B). UMAP visualization revealed a conserved cellular architecture without infection-induced clusters (Supplementary Fig. 13A), enabling direct comparison of preidentified macrophage subsets. A brief T/NKT analysis is provided in Supplementary Fig. 14. CellChat analysis showed that the number of inferred interactions was conserved across groups, whereas overall communication strength increased during acute infection, consistent with intensified intercellular signalling (Fig. 4C). Subcluster-specific communication strength analysis revealed NR1H3_Macro as a major signalling hub and cytokine source, with sharply increased incoming and outgoing interaction strength at 3 dpi (Fig. 4D). By contrast, IRF8_Macro showed reduced communication strength (Fig. 4D). Pathway analysis indicated activation of IFNG signalling (Supplementary Fig. 13B), with IFNG_NKT cells acting as senders and NR1H3_Macro as receivers via IFNGR1/2 (Supplementary Fig. 13D). NR1H3_Macro also transitioned towards a TNF-secreting phenotype and emerged as a key sender through TNF–TNFRSF1B interactions (Supplementary Fig. 13C). Although the abundance of NR1H3_Macro and IRF8_Macro remained stable across infection stages (Fig. 4E, F), their transcriptional states diverged. UCell scoring using subset-specific markers showed attenuation of anti-inflammatory signatures in NR1H3_Macro, whereas IRF8_Macro scores unchanged (Fig. 4G). Consistently, differential expression analysis within NR1H3_Macro revealed infection-induced downregulation of NR1H3 together with upregulation of proinflammatory mediators (IL1B, TNF, TNFSF9 and TNFSF14) and complement components (C1QA, C1QB and C1QC) (Fig. 4H, I). These results suggest that NR1H3 acts as a rheostat that constrains macrophage inflammatory potential, and its suppression permits inflammatory activation.

Conservation of NR1H3-mediated immunosuppression in human macrophages

Given the prominence of NR1H3⁺ macrophages in tree shrew, we asked whether a similar population exists in humans and exhibits conserved functions. NR1H3+ macrophages have been identified in human spleen scRNA-seq datasets43, and their expression profiles correlated with those of tree shrew (r=0.769, p < 0.01) (Fig. 5A, B, Supplementary Fig. 15), supporting conserved functions. To test function, we generated human NR1H3-overexpressing (NR1H3-OE) and NR1H3-knockdown (NR1H3-KO) THP-1 cell lines using lentivirus transduction system (Fig. 5C). Both NR1H3-OE and NR1H3-KO THP-1 cells differentiated normally, indicating that NR1H3 gain or NR1H3 loss of function did not grossly alter THP-1 macrophage differentiation (Fig. 5D). In functional assays, NR1H3 gain in THP‑1 macrophages reduced secretion of IL‑1β, IL‑6 and TNF‑α, modestly decreased uptake of bacterial particles, and diminished IFN‑γ production and effector polarization of primary CD8⁺ T cells while leaving T‑cell proliferation unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 17A–F). Furthermore, pharmacologic activation of NR1H3 with T0901317 in primary human monocyte‑derived macrophages similarly suppressed LPS‑induced IL‑1β, TNF‑α and IL‑6 release (Supplementary Fig. 17G, H), underscoring the translational relevance of NR1H3‑mediated immunoregulation.

We next performed bulk RNA-seq on NR1H3-OE and wild-type (WT) cells. Consistent with findings in the tree shrew model, TNF (log FoldChange = -1.73, p < 0.01), TNFSF14 (log FoldChange = -0.88, p < 0.01), and C1QA (log FoldChange = -1.37, p = 0.04) were downregulated in NR1H3-OE macrophages (Fig. 5E and Supplementary Data 3). Furthermore, key non-canonical NF-κB pathway-associated genes, including NFKBIZ (log FoldChange = -0.77, p = 0.02), NFKB2 (log FoldChange = -1.29, p < 0.01), and MAP3K14 (log FoldChange = -1.36, p < 0.01), were also repressed (Fig. 5E). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using the Reactome database showed negative enrichment of REACTOME_TNF_RECEPTOR_SUPERFAMILY_TNFSF_MEMBERS_MEDIATING_NON_CANONICAL_NF_KB_PATHWAY in NR1H3-OE macrophages (NES=-1.49, p = 0.047) (Fig. 5F and Supplementary Data 4). Altered expression of selected genes was validated by qRT–PCR (Fig. 5G). To test whether NR1H3 directly binds to these loci, we performed NR1H3 cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis (Fig. 5H and Supplementary Data 5). At NR1H3-OE-induced gene loci, NR1H3 binding was detected upstream of TNFSF14, NFKB2 and NFKBIZ (Fig. 5I). We further evaluated pharmacological activation using two NR1H3 agonists (T0901317 and GW3965) 44,45. These agonists increased NR1H3 protein abundance in THP-1 macrophages (Fig. 5J). Consistent with NR1H3-mediated repression, agonist-dependent suppression of TNFSF14, NFKB2 and NFKBIZ was attenuated in NR1H3-KO THP-1 macrophages (Fig. 5K), supporting an NR1H3-dependent mechanism.

Cross-species integration highlights tree shrew as a phylogenetic bridge

Given the conserved role of NR1H3 in human and tree shrew macrophages, we investigated whether the identified regulatory mechanism represents a broader feature preserved across vertebrate evolution. To minimise confounding effects of tissue microenvironment-driven specialization, we focused on splenic macrophages. We integrated publicly available spleen scRNA-seq data across seven vertebrate species (GEO accession GSE186158), including primates (human and macaque), a close relative of primates (tree shrew), and commonly used experimental models spanning diverse lineages (pigs, rats, mice, and zebrafish). After quality control, the integrated map consisted of 88,106 cells (approximately 10,000 cells for each species), and was annotated into four major immune lineages based on canonical markers (Fig. 6A-B, Supplementary Fig. 18A). To compare cross‑species macrophage programs, we generated pseudobulk profiles by aggregating splenic macrophages within each species to reduce technical noise, and performed multidimensional scaling (MDS) on these profiles. The MDS projection broadly reflected phylogenetic relationships and positioned tree shrew between rodents and primates (Fig. 6C).

We first identified a core set of conserved macrophage genes broadly expressed across species, including CSF1R, NR1H3, CFP, CTSB, PSAP, LGMN, and ASAH1. CSF1R showed consistent expression across all species (Fig. 6D and E). NR1H3 expression varied across datasets, with low expression in mouse macrophages compared with higher expression in human and tree shrew macrophages (Fig. 6E). We next examined conservation of functional macrophage programs. Cytokine-related gene sets (IL1B, IL4R, IL10RA, TGFB1, IFNAR1, IFNGR1, TNFAIP8, TNFRSF14, and TNFRSF1B) were broadly conserved across species, with zebrafish showing a reduced set (TNFRSF14 and TGFB1). Chemokine gene (CCL4, CCL5, CXCR4, CXCL10, and CXCL16) showed closer similarity between tree shrew and human than between macaque and human in this dataset, differing mainly at CCL5. Complement-related genes (C1QA, C1QB, C1QBP, and C1QC) were largely conserved (Fig. 6E). To further explore the species-specific transcriptional features, we applied high-dimensional weighted gene coexpression network analysis (hdWGCNA)47 and identified 23 modules (Supplementary Fig. 18 B, C, Supplementary Data 6). We computed Pearson correlations between module genes and species labels, and designated the module with the highest correlation coefficient as the signature module for each species (Fig. 6F). Species-specific module genes were subjected to GO enrichment analysis using topGO (v2.38.1) (Fig. 6G and Supplementary Fig. 18 D). Although each species exhibited distinct functional characteristics associated with its macrophage-specific modules, many enriched terms converged on immune development and inflammatory pathways. Together, these results highlight both conservation and divergence of splenic macrophage programmes across vertebrates and support the tree shrew as a phylogenetically intermediate model for studying human-relevant immunological mechanisms.
