## Methods

Ethics statement

For the multi-organ single-cell atlas, tissues were collected from three adult tree shrews (two males and one female; 8 months old; 120.5 ± 4.3 g). For the EBV infection experiments, twelve tree shrews (8 months old; 123.1 ± 7.6 g) were randomly assigned to the 3 dpi and 7 dpi groups (n = 6 per group; three males and three females per group), and tissues were collected at the indicated time points. All tree shrews were housed separately in a semi-barrier facility at 23°C–25°C and 40%–50% humidity under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle, with ad libitum access to standard chow and water60. All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Ethics Review Committee of Guangxi Medical University (approval no. 202101025) and were conducted in accordance with the Guiding Principles for the Use and Care of Experimental Animals issued by the Ministry of Science and Technology of China. Animals were euthanized by overdose of sodium pentobarbital followed by cervical dislocation prior to tissue collection.

Human peripheral blood samples were obtained from three healthy adult volunteers (two males and one female; 23-25 years old) for PBMC isolation. All participants provided written informed consent, and all uses of human material were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (approval no. 2025-E0760). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant local regulations.

Tissue dissociation and sample preparation for single-nucleus/cell library generation

Tissues were collected from 12 different samples: the spleen, thymus, tonsil, lymph nodes, nasopharynx, marrow, PBMCs, lung, liver, heart, kidney and stomach. Parenchymal tissues (except liver and heart) were placed in prechilled Hanks’ balanced salt solution (HBSS, Thermo Fisher Scientific) immediately after dissection. Samples were sliced into 3-4 mm3 pieces and digested into a cell suspension using digestion buffer containing 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Sigma‒Aldrich) and 1 mg/mL collagenase II (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were passed through a 70 μm strainer to remove the undigested tissue and centrifuged at 300 ×g for 5 min at 4 °C. Pelleted cells were resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (Solarbio) and incubated for 1 min at 4 °C. After washing twice with DPBS (Gibco), cell pellets were resuspended in sorting buffer (DPBS supplemented with 1% FBS). To mitigate dissociation-associated bias for large or fragile cells61, snRNA-seq was performed on liver and heart. Single-cell suspensions were captured in 10 × Genomics Chromium Single-Cell 5’ Solution, and single nuclei were captured in 10 × Genomics Chromium Single-cell 3’ Solution. The scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq library was generated by Beijing Novogene Company and prepared following the manufacturer’s protocol.

Raw data processing

Raw reads were aligned to the tree shrew reference genome (TupChi_1.0; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000334495.1/) using the Cell Ranger v6.1.0 pipeline (10 × Genomics) with default parameters, followed by barcode assignment and unique molecular identifier (UMI) counting. Filtered count matrices were imported into Seurat (v4.0.0)62 for downstream processing. Potential doublets were detected and filtered using DoubletFinder63 with default parameters. The cells/nuclei were filtered on the basis of a minimal expression threshold of 500 genes and 1000 UMIs, as well as genes that were expressed in at least five cells/nuclei. To remove outliers, we discarded cells in the bottom 1% and top 1% of the gene and UMI distributions per library, and removed cells/nuclei with more than 30% mitochondrial counts. Filtered data were normalized with Seurat’s NormalizeData function and highly variable features (n = 2000) were selected using the “vst” method. Datasets across organs and modalities (scRNA‑seq/snRNA‑seq) were integrated using Seurat’s RPCA anchor‑based workflow. We computed 20 principal components (“RunPCA”) to mitigate batch effects, and generated a UMAP embedding for visualization. Clustering was performed using shared nearest neighbour graph clustering (Louvain community detection-based method) with “FindClusters” at resolution of 1.2. Cell types were annotated in two stages. First, major cell classes (immune, endothelial, epithelial, fibroblast, and parenchymal compartments) were assigned using canonical markers and cluster-defining genes identified with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (default parameters). Second, immune‑cell subtypes were assigned using CellTypist (model: “Immune_All_High.pkl”; default settings) after mapping tree shrew genes to their human orthologs. Final labels were derived by a cluster‑level majority‑voting rule subject to a pre‑specified label‑probability threshold; cells not meeting this threshold were retained as “unassigned” and subsequently curated using canonical markers. Non‑immune subtypes were annotated using curated tissue‑specific marker panels from the literature and cross‑validated against the “FindAllMarkers”. Representative marker profiles for the 39 annotated cell types are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

Gene regulatory network construction

A list of tree shrew transcription factors was downloaded from AnimalTFDB3.064. We applied SCENIC (v0.10.0) to infer regulatory networks. TF-target pairs with weight values greater than 0.01 were retained to define coexpression modules. AUCell scores were computed to quantify regulon activity in each cell. The final cell type- and tissue-specific gene regulatory networks were visualized in Cytoscape 3.7.2 (https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape).

Cell–cell interaction analysis

Interactions among different cell types were predicted with the CellChat package (v1.1.3) based on curated ligand‒receptor pairs. Tree shrew genes were mapped to human orthologues (reciprocal best-hit BLASTP; Supplementary Data 7) to enable use of the human database. CellChatDB.human was used as the interaction database. The communication probabilities were calculated with the “computeCommunProb”, enriched ligand–receptor pairs were extracted using “extractEnrichedLR”. In addition, global communication patterns and signal networks were analysed using the built-in nonnegative matrix factorisation framework. Interactions with P value < 0.05 were considered significance.

Cross‑species comparisons

Public single-cell datasets for human, macaque, pigs, rats, mice, and zebrafish were obtained from the GEO database (accession number GSE186158) and processed using the same QC and normalization strategy prior to integration. For cross‑species analysis we restricted integration to spleen to minimize tissue‑driven heterogeneity and maintain consistency with the rest of the study. Orthologs were defined by reciprocal best‑hit BLAST of translated peptides against the human proteome; only one‑to‑one orthologs shared by all species were retained and gene identifiers were harmonized to human symbols (Supplementary Data 7). For each species, count matrices were processed in Seurat with SCTransform normalization, then performed integration using Seurat’s canonical correlation analysis (CCA) with default parameters. For between‑species transcriptomic similarity, we computed per‑species macrophage pseudobulk profiles, calculated Euclidean distances, and applied classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) to obtain the first two dimensions shown in the MDS plot46.

Statistical analysis

Data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise stated. Two-sided statistical tests were used throughout unless indicated. For two group comparisons, unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used for approximately normally distributed data; otherwise the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used. For comparisons involving more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (or Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s test for non-parametric data) was applied. Where multiple hypotheses were tested (e.g., differential expression, enrichment analyses), P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and FDR < 0.05 was considered significant unless stated otherwise.

Data availability

The scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq and Cut&Tag data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1051046 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1051046). Human splenic scRNA-seq was obtained from the Tissue Immune Cell Atlas portal (https://www.tissueimmunecellatlas.org/#datasets). Public datasets used for cross-species analyses were obtained from GEO (accession GSE186158). Source data are provided with this paper. Primer sequences and antibodies used in this study are provided in Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Table 2, respectively.

Code availability

The custom code used in this study is available at https://github.com/xialabtools/Tree_shrew_scRNA_code. This repository has been archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17609696).

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript the authors analysed by single cell high-throughput RNA-seq several tissues from a small rodents (T.belangeri). The animal model was chosen because of a relatively higher similarity to humans with respect to mice and rats. Despite the inherently interesting findings regarding the tree shrew's immune system and its potential as a more representative model for human immunity, we have significant concerns regarding the reproducibility and the comprehensive functional validation of the study. The identification of human-like immune features, such as the tonsillar structure and the conserved NR1H3+ macrophage subset, is compelling, and the proposed role of these macrophages in EBV infection is particularly noteworthy.

However, few critical issues must be addressed to solidify the study’s impact.

General comments:
Insufficient Bioinformatics Pipeline Details and Reproducibility
Our primary concern lies with the insufficient description and accessibility of the bioinformatics pipeline. While the provided "Raw data processing" section offers a good start by detailing some steps, it lacks the comprehensive transparency needed for true reproducibility, especially for complex single-cell analyses. The paper outlines exciting discoveries, but without a complete understanding and direct access to the computational methods used, it's impossible for other researchers to independently verify or build upon these findings.

Specifically, while the authors have listed some software and parameters, they need to provide a far more thorough and transparent account of their bioinformatics approach. This includes, but is not limited to:
Custom Scripting and Workflows: The M&M section mentions specific packages and functions, but often single-cell analysis involves custom scripts to integrate these tools, perform specific filtering steps, or generate custom visualizations. These scripts, and the order in which they are executed, are crucial for replication.

Cell Type Annotation Strategy: A total of 39 cell types were identified in this paper, but the M&M section doesn't detail how these cell types were assigned. Was it based on known marker gene expression? Were external reference atlases used for annotation? This is a critical step that needs clear explanation.

Specifics of Cross-Species Comparison for CellChat: While it states "homologous gene mapping from T. belangeri to the human genome was first performed to identify the corresponding genes in humans," the method or tool used for this homologous mapping (e.g., BLAST, Ensembl Compara, custom ortholog tables) is missing. This is vital for the validity of the cross-species comparison in CellChat.

Version Control and Environment Management: Simply listing software versions is helpful, but the exact computational environment (e.g., operating system, specific R/Python versions, library dependencies) in which the analysis was performed is essential for ensuring that code runs without dependency conflicts or unexpected behavior.

Critically, to fully address the issue of reproducibility, I strongly recommend that the authors provide a link to a publicly accessible GitHub repository containing the complete analysis code. This repository should ideally be structured to allow for step-by-step execution of the analysis, from raw data processing to the generation of figures. Even better, the provision of a Docker container encapsulating the entire computational environment and analysis pipeline would be the gold standard.
This would allow any researcher to precisely replicate the computational steps and ensure the robustness of the reported findings, without encountering issues related to software installations or versioning.

2. Lack of Functional Validation for NR1H3 Activation
While the provided results presented in the paragraph “Conservation of NR1H3-mediated immunosuppression in human macrophages” demonstrate a strong correlation between NR1H3 activation and the downregulation of pro-inflammatory and non-canonical NF-KB pathway genes in THP-1 cells, it primarily focuses on transcriptional changes and direct binding. This is a valuable step, but it doesn't definitively prove the functional consequence of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression at a cellular or immunological level.

To demonstrate the "true functionality" of NR1H3 activation in immunosuppression, especially in the context of human macrophages, the following experiments would be helpful
a. Functional Assays on Macrophage Pro-inflammatory Responses:
Cytokine and chemokine Production Assays:
Measure secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines (using ELISA or multiplex cytokine arrays) upon stimulation with PAMPs/DAMPs from challenge NR1H3-OE, NR1H3-KO, and WT THP-1 cells
NR1H3 activation should lead to a reduction in these cytokines compared to WT or NR1H3-KO cells.
Phagocytosis Assay: While not directly linked to inflammation, some immunosuppressive macrophages might have altered phagocytic capabilities. This could be an exploratory experiment.

b. Immune cell crosstalk assays:
Co-culture Experiments with T cells (or other immune cells) can also give useful insight and functional readout. Therefore, a T cell Proliferation Assay can be performed to depict the biological consequences of NR1H3 activation. Likewise, the authors can investigate the T cell Cytokine Production and cell Differentiation

c. In Vivo Relevance/Translational Experiments (if feasible):
Ex vivo stimulation of human primary macrophages: If possible, obtain human primary macrophages (e.g., from PBMCs) and activate NR1H3 pharmacologically (with T0901317 or GW3965). Then, repeat the cytokine/chemokine production assays after inflammatory stimulation. This would bridge the gap from THP-1 cells to primary human
By incorporating these functional assays, the authors would move beyond solely demonstrating transcriptional changes and direct gene binding to definitively prove the "true functionality" of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression in human macrophages. This would significantly strengthen their claim about the conserved anti-inflammatory immunoregulatory function of NR1H3.

Specific comments:
1. The observed-to-expected cell ratios (Ro/e) presented in Fig 1 and Fig3D is not clear. What is the expected cell number? From which dataset does this derive? Wasn’t it worth to compare different tissues across themselves? As it is in this current version, the plot is not meaningful
2. Fig 5A/B. The human/T.belangeri macrophage similarity is unclear and not convincing. What exactly is represented in Fig 5B? What is each dot? It is indeed difficult to state the “similarity”similarity”” between two cell types in different organs, unless many cells are compared and the two in exams are more close to each other with respect to the distance between other cells.

Minor comments:
In the text, the experimental strategy is not clearly presented. The reader expects to have 36 samples, 12 tissues from three animals, but only 24 samples are actually there (3 for immune organs, one for other and one for pharyngeal tonsil). This must be better addressed at the beginning of the results.
The differences between gender is not analyzed in any of the main or supplementary figures. As there might be gender differences it is worth to analyze it and, especially for tissues where one single organ was processed, it is worth mentioning from which animal they were processed.
Fig 3e, the GO dot plot should be on the right of the GO terms, otherwise it seems the dots refers to the genes on the left

### Reviewer 2

This study by Tang and colleagues presents a comprehensive single-cell immune cell atlas of Tupaia belangeri and provides compelling evidence that the tree shrew is a promising model organism for immunological research. By integrating multi-tissue profiling, EBV infection modeling, and cross-species comparisons, the authors effectively demonstrate the translational potential of Tupaia, particularly in contexts where conventional rodent models are limited.

Importance:
The study is meaningful in that it establishes a foundational resource for using Tupaia belangeri as a non-primate animal model. Its evolutionary proximity to humans and permissiveness to human-specific pathogens make it particularly valuable for translational studies, especially in the field of viral immunology.

Specific comments:
1. Data processing rigor:
Several aspects of data processing and integration require clearer explanation. For instance, how doublets were removed, what specific QC metrics were applied, and how batch effects were corrected are not sufficiently described. Given the inclusion of multiple tissues and time points, this methodological clarity is essential.
More specifically, the localization of T cells in Supplementary Fig. 1 appears questionable, suggesting that doublet removal may not have been adequately performed. Epithelial cell annotations also appear inconsistent across figures. I recommend the authors include UMAP plots annotated by major cell types (e.g., T cells, B cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts) to improve transparency.
Furthermore, batch correction and integration should be benchmarked using multiple methods (e.g., Harmony, scVI) rather than relying on a single approach.

2. Depth of analysis in the EBV model:
The EBV infection model is an important part of the study, but the analysis feels relatively shallow. For example, was EBV transcript detected in B cells or other cell types? Basic analyses such as pseudotime trajectory, cell type-specific differential gene expression (DEG), and pathway enrichment should be provided before diving into cell–cell communication analysis.
Additionally, recent tools like Milo could be combined with improved integration methods to track graph-level changes in cell proportions.

Minor comment: In Supplementary Fig. 13A, the temporal order should be displayed as Control → Day 3 → Day 7. Also, the terms “Pos-macro” and “Neg-macro” are not clearly defined and are inconsistent with previous labeling.

3. Cross-species comparison methodology:
The cross-species integration is one of the more exciting aspects of this paper, but its current implementation is too preliminary. Key technical steps—such as ortholog selection, normalization across species, and gene filtering—should be explained in more detail. Methods like SATURN or scGLUE could be applied here to improve both the interpretability and robustness of the analysis.
In particular, the MDS plot is difficult to interpret, and it is unclear what the axes represent. If this plot is intended to convey evolutionary distance or transcriptional similarity, it should be supplemented with more formal statistical support.
Additionally, the analysis of HLA loci, which are known to be highly divergent between species, needs to be handled with extra caution. Ortholog mapping for HLA genes should be genome-informed and well-documented.

### Reviewer 4

This new study describes a single cell immune atlas for the tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri). Tree shrews are an emerging small animal model that are evolutionarily closer to primates than mice. As such, tree shrews represent a useful, viable alternative model for infectious disease and aging studies that may be otherwise challenging to carryout in murine or non-human primate model systems. The investigators profiled single cells from 12 different tissues of 3 adult tree shrews, identifying 39 different cell types. Notably, bulk RNAseq studies have been performed in spleen, PBMCs, and other tissues from the tree shrew, and single cell transcriptome atlases have been recently published for brain and neurological tissues. A strength of this study is that it represents the first tree shrew immune-focused single cell atlas which can provide an important platform for understanding systemic transcriptional responses to infectious diseases in future studies. Aside from the substantial efforts that went into generating this resource, there are some key weaknesses and major concerns with the overall conclusions derived from the interpretation of the EBV infection data.

Major Concerns:
1. Atlas reveals that T.belangeri possess well-developed tonsillar structures analogous to human tonsils. These tonsillar anatomical structures within the oropharynx were previously reported for the tree shrew—and thus, it is expected that these tissues will harbor lymphoid cell types commonly observed in primate tonsils. However, in figure 1, mature and activated B cell subsets are not detected in the pharyngeal tonsils, which is unusual. Could this be due to sampling issues or issues with adequate sequencing coverage? As the tonsils are a significant focus of the paper (Fig 2), more work needs to be put into describing these cells. Fig. 2B needs to be described in detail—UMAP represents cells in which tonsils? There were only ~2700 cells sequenced for pharyngeal—were palantine and pharyngeal grouped together in this figure? Are the cell subsets and relative distributions of representative cell types in these tissues comparable to what is reported in human and nonhuman primate samples?

2. A major caveat is that the EBV infection model does not mimic natural oral uptake and natural viral transmission which is observed in other NHP models with LCVs (i.e. rhesus and cynomolgus macaque models). Here, the route of EBV administration is intravenous into the femoral vein, thus any relevance to palantine/pharyngeal tonsil responses—which the authors argue is an important component of the tree shrew model (Fig. 2)—is unclear as this requires trafficking of the virus to the oral/throat cavity (in previous publications with this tree shrew model, EBV shedding occurs at 7 dpi). It is unclear why tonsil cells were not sequenced from the infected animals as this would highlight the importance and biological relevance of these structures for EBV infection. The I.V. infection route and also the high titer virus administered is akin to what is utilized in mouse models, which does not recapitulate natural EBV infection in humans and this needs to be acknowledged. As such, the immune responses (i.e. bypassing mucosal immunity in the oral cavity and gut that occurs with oral challenge) are expected to be skewed.

3. The sample size for EBV experiments in Fig 4 is extremely small. Spleen cells are sequenced from only two animals that were infected with EBV and harvested at different time points, limiting the statistical power and generalizability of findings that NR1H3(LXRa+) macrophages are indeed altered by EBV infection. It is basically a pilot experiment. In an attempt to confirm scRNAseq findings, immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR experiments were performed on samples from 4 animals in Fig 4. No differences in NR1H3+ or IRF8+ macrophage numbers were detected by IFA, although the NR1H3 RNA level does decrease, which hardly confirms the scRNAseq findings. Given that data describing NR1H3 cell reprogramming is from n=1, additional evidence should be provided to support the major conclusions that NRH13+ macrophages dominate the inflammatory responses observed in EBV infection. For example, does depletion of these cells impact acute EBV infection? Are there additional signs of inflammatory markers that track with these macrophage subsets?

4. Depletion of liver X receptors (NR1H3 gene encodes LXRa) in mice leads to enhanced replication of a murine g-herpesvirus (MHV68) that is often used as a model for EBV infection (PMC6050960). Such prior studies indicate NRH13-mediated mechanisms are indeed conserved in mice.

5. The study largely focuses on describing B cells and macrophage subset, yet T cell responses are a major contributor to control of infectious agents that have been tested in tree shrew models (i.e. Zika, hepatitis virus). T cell populations should be described in detail.

Other minor comments:
1. Introduction, line 52: smaller NHPs such as marmosets and tamarins have been historically used for EBV infection studies and should be mentioned in this section.
2. Line 74, first single-cell atlas of T. belangeri and line 435: This is incorrectly stated as there are at least three other publications describing brain/neurological tissue-focused single cell atlases for the tree shrew.

Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need to clarify our annotation strategy. We implemented a two-stage procedure: (i) We first separated major classes using canonical markers (e.g., immune vs. non-immune; endothelial, epithelial, fibroblast, parenchymal) at the cluster level, guided by cluster-defining genes identified with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (default parameters). This step leverages the marker framework already described in the manuscript and summarized across the 39 cell types. (ii) Immune compartment: we applied CellTypist1 (model “Immune_All_High.pkl”, default settings) after mapping tree shrew genes to human orthologs, and adopted cluster‑level majority voting with a label‑probability threshold to retain only high‑confidence labels. Non‑immune compartment: we used curated organ‑specific canonical markers from the literature to assign labels and cross‑checked them with the FindAllMarkers outputs. Ambiguous clusters were flagged for manual curation. For transparency, the full per‑cluster marker tables, annotation scripts, and execution order are provided in our public repository/Zenodo snapshot (see Code Availability). The final set of 39 annotated cell types and representative marker patterns is summarized in Supplementary Fig. 3, which supports the validity of our labels.

2. Lack of Functional Validation for NR1H3 Activation
While the provided results presented in the paragraph “Conservation of NR1H3-mediated immunosuppression in human macrophages” demonstrate a strong correlation between NR1H3 activation and the downregulation of pro-inflammatory and non-canonical NF-KB pathway genes in THP-1 cells, it primarily focuses on transcriptional changes and direct binding. This is a valuable step, but it doesn't definitively prove the functional consequence of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression at a cellular or immunological level. To demonstrate the “true functionality” of NR1H3 activation in immunosuppression, especially in the context of human macrophages, the following experiments would be helpful.
(a) Functional Assays on Macrophage Pro-inflammatory Responses: (1) Cytokine and chemokine Production Assays: Measure secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines (using ELISA or multiplex cytokine arrays) upon stimulation with PAMPs/DAMPs from challenge NR1H3-OE, NR1H3-KO, and WT THP-1 cells. NR1H3 activation should lead to a reduction in these cytokines compared to WT or NR1H3-KO cells.
Response: Thank you for this constructive suggestion. We added a cytokine‑secretion assay to test whether NR1H3 activation suppresses macrophage inflammatory cytokines. Specifically, we challenged WT, NR1H3‑overexpressing (OE), and NR1H3‑knockout (KO) THP‑1–derived macrophages with a standardized PAMP stimulus and quantified secreted IL‑1β, IL‑6, and TNF‑α in culture supernatants by ELISA (Elabscience, China); absorbance was read at 450 nm on a BioTek microplate reader with on‑plate standards confirming good linearity (R² > 0.98). Across n=4 biological replicates per group and one‑way ANOVA with post‑hoc testing, NR1H3‑OE cells released significantly less IL‑1β, IL‑6, and TNF‑α than WT and KO (P < 0.01 for each cytokine). KO vs WT showed a significant increase for IL‑1β (P < 0.01) and no significant change for IL‑6/TNF‑α under this strong stimulus (likely a ceiling effect) (RFigure 1). These secretion data provide the requested functional readout and are consistent with our human‑cell mechanism showing NR1H3‑dependent repression of TNF and NF‑κB genes (NFKB2, NFKBIZ, MAP3K14) with direct NR1H3 binding, thereby linking molecular repression and reduced effector cytokines in human macrophages.

Middle: standard curves with linear regression and R² (IL-1β: 0.9925; IL-6: 0.9954; TNF-α: 0.9876). Right: cytokine quantification (mean ± SD, n=4); P < 0.01 indicated by **, “ns” denotes not significant (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests).
(2) Phagocytosis Assay: While not directly linked to inflammation, some immunosuppressive macrophages might have altered phagocytic capabilities. This could be an exploratory experiment.
Response: To explore whether NR1H3 activation alters macrophage effector functions, we compared phagocytosis in WT vs NR1H3‑overexpressing (OE) THP‑1–derived macrophages. THP‑1 cells (5×105/mL) were differentiated with PMA 100 ng/mL for 24 h, then incubated 4 h with pHrodo™ Red E. coli bioparticles (Thermo Fisher; 1:100 v/v; reagent resuspended in PBS and sonicated 5 min). Phagocytosed particles (fluorescent in acidified phagosomes) were visualized by confocal microscopy and quantified by flow cytometry. NR1H3‑OE cells showed a lower pHrodo‑positive fraction than WT (representative gates: WT = 91.6%, OE = 64.4%), with a significant reduction in phagocytic cells (P < 0.01, unpaired two‑tailed t‑test; mean ± SD; independent experiments shown as dots)( RFigure 2).
These data suggest NR1H3 activation modestly dampens phagocytic uptake, complementing our molecular evidence that NR1H3 enforces an immunoregulatory program in human macrophages.
RFigure 2: NR1H3 activation reduces phagocytosis of pHrodo‑labeled bacteria in THP‑1 macrophages. (A) Phase‑contrast/fluorescence overlays of WT and NR1H3‑OE cells exposed to pHrodo Red E. coli (red). (B) Confocal images (DAPI, blue; pHrodo, red). (C) Representative flow‑cytometry histograms showing gated pHrodo‑positive fractions (left: WT + E. coli; right: OE + E. coli) and summary quantification (right panel; mean ± SD). ** P < 0.01; unpaired two‑tailed t‑test. Response: To test whether NR1H3 activation in human macrophages functionally skews T‑cell responses, we isolated CD3⁺ T cells from healthy donors (written consent; Ethics 2025‑E0760) and stimulated them with PHA in the presence of conditioned supernatants from either WT‑THP‑1 or NR1H3‑overexpressing (OE) THP‑1 macrophages. IFN‑γ output was measured by ELISPOT; T‑cell effector polarization was assessed by intracellular IFN‑γ staining within CD8⁺ T cells using a standard Fc‑block, surface stain, fixation/permeabilization and intracellular staining on a CytoFLEX; and proliferation was quantified by CFSE dilution (RFigure 3A).
Results: NR1H3‑OE macrophage supernatant reduced IFN‑γ spots compared with WT (P<0.05) (RFigure 3B), and decreased the fraction of IFN‑γ⁺ CD8⁺ T cells (54.8% to 28.2%, P<0.01) (RFigure 3C), while proliferation was unchanged (CFSE, not significant) (RFigure 3D). Thus, NR1H3 activation in macrophages dampens T‑cell effector cytokine production/polarization without nonspecific suppression of clonal expansion, providing a clear cellular‑level consequence that is consistent with our demonstrated NR1H3‑dependent repression of inflammation function in human macrophages.

(A) Workflow schematic: donor PBMC isolation, CD3⁺ T‑cell negative selection, culture with WT or NR1H3‑OE THP‑1 conditioned supernatants during PHA stimulation, and ELISPOT/flow‑cytometry readouts. (D) CFSE‑based proliferation: overlaid histograms and quantification indicate no significant difference (n.s.).
(c) In Vivo Relevance/Translational Experiments (if feasible):
Ex vivo stimulation of human primary macrophages: If possible, obtain human primary macrophages (e.g., from PBMCs) and activate NR1H3 pharmacologically (with T0901317 or GW3965). Then, repeat the cytokine/chemokine production assays after inflammatory stimulation. This would bridge the gap from THP-1 cells to primary human
Response: To extend our findings from THP‑1 cells to primary human cells, we isolated PBMCs from healthy donors with written consent and ethics approval 2025‑E0760. Total monocytes were purified by negative selection and differentiated into macrophages for 5 days with M‑CSF (50 ng/mL); adherent cells were then treated with the NR1H3 agonist T0901317 for 24 h, challenged with an inflammatory stimulus, and culture supernatants were assayed for IL‑1β, IL‑6, and TNF‑α by ELISA (Elabscience; OD 450 nm, BioTek) (RFigure 4A). Across independent donors, T0901317 significantly lowered all three cytokines compared with control macrophages (P < 0.01) (RFigure 4B). Together, these ex vivo human data demonstrate that pharmacologic NR1H3 activation suppresses primary macrophage inflammatory output, reinforcing the translational relevance of our THP‑1 and mechanistic results showing NR1H3‑dependent repression of TNF and non‑canonical NF‑κB programs in human macrophages.

(B) ELISA of T0901317‑activated macrophages (mean ± SD; dots represent independent experiments; *P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01).
By incorporating these functional assays, the authors would move beyond solely demonstrating transcriptional changes and direct gene binding to definitively prove the “true functionality” of NR1H3 activation in mediating immunosuppression in human macrophages. This would significantly strengthen their claim about the conserved anti-inflammatory immunoregulatory function of NR1H3.

1. The observed-to-expected cell ratios (Ro/e) presented in Fig 1 and Fig3D is not clear. What is the expected cell number? From which dataset does this derive? Wasn’t it worth to compare different tissues across themselves? As it is in this current version, the plot is not meaningful
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. In our study, the observed‑to‑expected ratio (Ro/e) quantifies tissue preference for each cell type under a common global baseline. For cell type i in tissue t, the expected count is defined as E = pi × Nt, where pi is the global proportion of that cell type computed from our i,t integrated dataset of all tissues in this study, and Nt is the total number of profiled cells in tissue t; the observed count Oi,t is the number of cells of type i in t. The enrichment ratio is Ro/e = O / E ; values > 1 indicate enrichment and <1 indicate i,t i,t i,t depletion. Thus, Ro/e explicitly compares tissues against each other for each cell type using a common global baseline, which is what our heatmaps visualize (e.g., Fig. 1D and Fig. 3D; thresholds noted in the legends to highlight strong preference). This formulation follows prior single-cell work (e.g., Zhang et al., Nature. 2018)3 and is referenced in our manuscript; we now make the formula and data source explicit in the text and figure legends for clarity.

Each dot in Fig. 5B corresponds to one ortholog‑matched gene (mean log‑normalized expression in human on one axis and in T. belangeri on the other). Remarks to the Author:
This study by Tang and colleagues presents a comprehensive single-cell immune cell atlas of Tupaia belangeri and provides compelling evidence that the tree shrew is a promising model organism for immunological research. By integrating multi-tissue profiling, EBV infection modeling, and cross-species comparisons, the authors effectively demonstrate the translational potential of Tupaia, particularly in contexts where conventional rodent models are limited.
Importance: The study is meaningful in that it establishes a foundational resource for using Tupaia belangeri as a non-primate animal model. Its evolutionary proximity to humans and permissiveness to human-specific pathogens make it particularly valuable for translational studies, especially in the field of viral immunology.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and supportive assessment of our study and for highlighting its translational value. We have revised the manuscript to further strengthen the evidence base and to improve clarity and transparency.
Specific comments:
1. Data processing rigor:
(a) Several aspects of data processing and integration require clearer explanation. For instance, how doublets were removed, what specific QC metrics were applied, and how batch effects were corrected are not sufficiently described. Given the inclusion of multiple tissues and time points, this methodological clarity is essential.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s request for greater methodological clarity. We have revised the Methods to describe our preprocessing and integration workflow step‑by‑step and to ensure full reproducibility.
1. Doublet removal. For each library, putative multiplets were identified with DoubletFinder (artificial-nearest-neighbor strategy, default settings) and removed prior to any integration.
2. Quality control. Cells/nuclei were retained if they had ≥500 detected genes and ≥1,000 UMIs; genes were kept if expressed in ≥5 cells. Cells/nuclei with >30% mitochondrial reads were excluded. To remove outliers, we also discarded the bottom and top 1% of cells by gene and UMI counts per library. Normalization used NormalizeData and the top 2,000 variable genes were selected with FindVariableFeatures (vst).
3. Batch correction / integration. For the cross-organ atlas (scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq), datasets were integrated using Seurat’s RPCA anchor workflow (FindIntegrationAnchors/IntegrateData). We computed 20 PCs, embedded with UMAP, and clustered with an SNN-Louvain graph (FindClusters, resolution = 1.2). For the EBV spleen time-course (same tissue across conditions), we used SCTransform-based integration (SCT) following Seurat’s recommended pipeline to minimize condition-specific effects while preserving shared cell states.
4. Annotation. We implemented a two stage procedure: (i) We first separated major classes using canonical markers (e.g., immune vs. non immune; endothelial, epithelial, fibroblast, parenchymal) at the cluster level, guided by cluster defining genes identified with Seurat’s FindAllMarkers (default parameters). This step leverages the marker framework already described in the manuscript and summarized across the 39 cell types. (ii) Immune compartment: we applied CellTypist (model “Immune_All_High.pkl”, default settings) after mapping tree shrew genes to human orthologs, and adopted cluster‑level majority voting with a label‑probability threshold to retain only high‑confidence labels. Non‑immune compartment: we used curated organ‑specific canonical markers from the literature to assign labels and cross‑checked them with the FindAllMarkers outputs. Ambiguous clusters were flagged for manual curation. The final set of 39 annotated cell types and representative marker patterns is summarized in Supplementary Fig. 3, which supports the validity of our labels.
To facilitate independent replication, the full analysis pipeline (raw-data processing, QC/doublets, integration, clustering/annotation, cross-species comparisons, figure generation) is publicly available at our GitHub repository (https://github.com/xialabtools/Tree_shrew_scRNA_code). This repository has been archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17609696).

2. Depth of analysis in the EBV model:
(a) The EBV infection model is an important part of the study, but the analysis feels relatively shallow. For example, was EBV transcript detected in B cells or other cell types? Basic analyses such as pseudotime trajectory, cell type-specific differential gene expression (DEG), and pathway enrichment should be provided before diving into cell–cell communication analysis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and would like to clarify that our EBV challenge was designed primarily to induce an in vivo inflammatory environment for studying NR1H3⁺ macrophages, rather than to model EBV pathogenesis itself. In fact, our prior work established that tree shrews can be infected with EBV and mirror key aspects of human EBV infection (e.g., transient acute viremia followed by latent viral persistence)6,7. We built the present study on this established tree shrew EBV model to stimulate the immune system and highlight macrophage dynamics in an EBV-induced inflammatory context.
To strengthen the analysis, we have increased the number of animals per time point (now n = 3, 4, and 4 at baseline and two post-infection time points, respectively) to improve statistical power. We also added new in vivo and in vitro validation experiments (see updated Fig. 6 and Supp. Fig. 18) that confirm the activation and characteristics of the NR1H3⁺ macrophages in the EBV-challenged condition, bolstering the conclusions of the study.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions for deeper analysis of the single-cell EBV infection data. In response, we performed additional cell-type-specific differential gene expression (DEG) and pathway enrichment analyses with a focus on T cell populations (RFigure 13). These new analyses revealed a robust IFN-γ (IFNG) induction in T cells and an enrichment of a CD8⁺ T cell subset expressing CXCL8, indicative of an active antiviral T cell response. We also observed significant upregulation of viral response pathways at 3 days post-infection (dpi), consistent with early immune activation against EBV. These findings provide further context for the cell–cell communication results and underscore that T cells were engaged during early EBV infection.
Regarding the detection of EBV transcripts, we re-aligned our scRNA-seq reads to a combined Tupaia belangeri (tree shrew) + EBV reference genome (Cell Ranger pipeline). No EBV transcripts were detected in any cell type, even in B cells. We believe this lack of viral RNA detection is due to several factors, including: (1) Early time points: Our analysis focused on early infection (e.g., 3 dpi), which may precede robust lytic viral gene expression or abundant latent transcripts. (2) Tissue context: The spleen may not be the primary site of EBV replication at these early time points. Given our infection route (intravenous inoculation), the virus might primarily infect peripheral B cells or other tissues before seeding the spleen, resulting in low viral load in the sampled organ. (3) Technical constraints: Droplet-based scRNA-seq has limited sensitivity for low-abundance transcripts, especially for a large DNA virus like EBV. Many EBV transcripts (particularly latent RNAs like EBERs) are not polyadenylated or are expressed at low levels, making them difficult to capture with standard scRNA-seq library preparation and sequencing depth.
Finally, while we agree that analyses such as pseudotime trajectory mapping of infection could yield interesting insights, we respectfully note that a full trajectory analysis of EBV infection is beyond the scope of our macrophage-centered study. Our focus was to identify and characterize the NR1H3⁺ macrophages under an inflammatory condition induced by EBV, rather than to exhaustively chart the course of EBV infection per se. We consider the reviewer’s suggested trajectory and cell-type resolved analyses very valuable for understanding EBV pathogenesis and immune dynamics; and these will be better addressed in a dedicated future study.

3. Cross-species comparison methodology:
(a) The cross-species integration is one of the more exciting aspects of this paper, but its current implementation is too preliminary. Key technical steps—such as ortholog selection, normalization across species, and gene filtering—should be explained in more detail. Response: We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of methodological transparency in the cross‑species analysis. We have expanded the Methods to detail ortholog selection, normalization across species, and the integration workflow, and we provide all code and ortholog tables for full reproducibility.
1. Focused spleen tissue: To ensure functional comparability, we limited the cross-species analysis to spleen only, thereby reducing tissue heterogeneity across species.
2. Ortholog selection (gene filtering): Integration was restricted to genes with one-to-one orthologs shared by all species, identified via reciprocal best-hit BLASTP search. This filtering guarantees that only directly comparable genes were used across the datasets. This workflow is consistent with the practice for cross-species single-cell comparisons and has been used in similar contexts (e.g., Tarashansky et al., 20212). A complete ortholog table is provided in the Supplementary Table7.
3. Normalization and integration: We applied Seurat’s SCTransform (SCT) normalization to each dataset, then performed integration using Seurat’s standard SCT + canonical correlation analysis (CCA) pipeline: SelectIntegrationFeatures → PrepSCTIntegration → FindIntegrationAnchors (with normalization.method = “SCT”) → IntegrateData. The integrated UMAP visualization shows that cells cluster by celltype rather than by species, indicating batch effects arising from species differences were effectively corrected. In other words, different species cells overlap in the integrated embedding, confirming that the integration preserved biological signal (cell identity) while correcting technical differences between species (RFigure 15). The specific script have now released a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/xialabtools/Tree_shrew_scRNA_code).
4. Method validation: Anchor‑based SCT+CCA has been widely used in high‑impact cross‑species/cross‑cohort atlases and provides a robust solution for single‑modality RNA data, as in our study. Similar workflows have been used in high-impact single-cell studies, including a cross-primate cell atlas8 (Jung et al., Nature 2022) and a human immune cell atlas1 (Domínguez Conde et al., Science 2022), as well as in cross-species tumor microenvironment analyses9 (Elyada et al., Cancer Discovery 2019). If the reviewer or readers feel that employing the newer SATURN tool is still necessary, we are open to exploring it in future work. However, given the scope of our current study (focusing on one organ across species) and the successful outcome with CCA, we believe our chosen approach is sufficient for this analysis.

The classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) panel is intended as a qualitative ordination of transcriptional dissimilarity, not as an evolutionary distance. In other words, they depict relative transcriptional similarities among the species’ macrophage profiles – not a direct evolutionary distance metric. Each point represents the transcriptional profile of macrophages from one species, derived from pseudobulk gene expression aggregates (following the approach of Crowell et al., 20204), thereby minimizing the impact of technical noise and cellular outliers. Then, pairwise Euclidean distances (on log‑normalized, gene‑wise z‑scored expression) were then embedded by classical MDS. The axes (MDS1 and MDS2) in MDS plot are the first two dimensions from classical multidimensional scaling of inter-sample expression distances, analogous to principal components, which are data‑derived coordinates with no intrinsic units. Because MDS is a projection and cross‑species differences may reflect both biology and residual technical factors, we interpret this panel cautiously and restrict inference to spleen macrophages. In additionlly, we have refocused the MDS analysis on macrophages only, rather than displaying all four immune lineages together. This targeted approach reduces heterogeneity from other lineages and aligns the figure with our macrophage-centered narrative.

Remarks to the Author:
This new study describes a single cell immune atlas for the tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri). Tree shrews are an emerging small animal model that are evolutionarily closer to primates than mice. As such, tree shrews represent a useful, viable alternative model for infectious disease and aging studies that may be otherwise challenging to carryout in murine or non-human primate model systems. The investigators profiled single cells from 12 different tissues of 3 adult tree shrews, identifying 39 different cell types. Notably, bulk RNAseq studies have been performed in spleen, PBMCs, and other tissues from the tree shrew, and single cell transcriptome atlases have been recently published for brain and neurological tissues. A strength of this study is that it represents the first tree shrew immune-focused single cell atlas which can provide an important platform for understanding systemic transcriptional responses to infectious diseases in future studies. Aside from the substantial efforts that went into generating this resource, there are some key weaknesses and major concerns with the overall conclusions derived from the interpretation of the EBV infection data.
Response: We thank Reviewer for recognizing the value of the first immune‑focused single‑cell atlas of Tupaia belangeri and for the constructive critique of our EBV analysis. We have revised manuscript according to your suggestion. Our explanation to the comments point- by- point is as follow.
Major Concerns:
1. Atlas reveals that T.belangeri possess well-developed tonsillar structures analogous to human tonsils. These tonsillar anatomical structures within the oropharynx were previously reported for the tree shrew—and thus, it is expected that these tissues will harbor lymphoid cell types commonly observed in primate tonsils.
(a) In figure 1, mature and activated B cell subsets are not detected in the pharyngeal tonsils, which is unusual. Could this be due to sampling issues or issues with adequate sequencing coverage?
Response: We agree that the apparent absence of mature and activated B cell subsets in the pharyngeal tonsil is unexpected. We believe this reflects sampling limitations rather than sequencing coverage. The pharyngeal tonsil is located deep near the skull base (RFigure 16) and was technically difficult to harvest; despite intending to sample three animals, only one specimen yielded sufficient tissue for scRNA‑seq. With this limited input, rare lymphocyte states are likely under‑represented even though per‑cell quality was adequate.
Notably, we still detected B cells (6.7%) and plasma cells (3.7%) in the pharyngeal tonsil. To verify that germinal‑center B cells were present in the tissue but missed at low frequency in scRNA‑seq, we performed immunohistochemistry, which showed BCL6⁺ (germinal‑center) and CR2/CD21⁺ B cells in pharyngeal‑tonsil sections (Supplementary Fig. 11). We have clarified in the text that the tonsil data represent a baseline anatomical/cellular atlas; the lower representation of mature/activated B‑cell subsets in this particular pharyngeal sample is most plausibly a sampling issue rather than a biological absence.

Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s question. No—palatine and pharyngeal tonsil datasets were analyzed and visualized independently throughout. As shown in Fig. 1B, the pharyngeal tonsil dataset contained ~2,700 cells, whereas the palatine tonsil dataset comprised ~14,700 cells; accordingly, Fig. 2B displays only the palatine tonsil UMAP, and the pharyngeal tonsil results are presented in Supplementary Fig. 11. Pharyngeal tonsil cells were analyzed separately and are shown in Supplementary Fig. 11.
(d) Are the cell subsets and relative distributions of representative cell types in these tissues comparable to what is reported in human and nonhuman primate samples?
Response: We agree that it is important to benchmark tree‑shrew tonsillar biology against human/NHP data. Across three orthogonal evidence, we find broad concordance:
1. Anatomy and H&E morphology. The tree shrew (T. belangeri) palatine tonsils are located in the lateral oropharynx (RFigure 17), and a pharyngeal tonsil resides in the nasopharyngeal roof, forming a Waldeyer’s ring equivalent, just as in primates. These tonsillar tissues lie adjacent to the airway and digestive tract, analogous to human tonsillar anatomy and differs from rodents like rodents that lack true tonsils11. Histological sections reveal numerous lymphoid follicles with germinal centers (GCs) beneath specialized epithelia, mirroring the fundamental organization in human tonsils12. In the palatine tonsil, a stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinized) covers deep invaginating crypts, underlain by dense follicles. This is identical to human palatine tonsils, which feature crypt epithelium and follicle-rich lymphoid tissue for antigen trapping13. We also note the germinal center morphology in tree shrew tonsils is highly characteristic: pale GC zones with dark peripheral mantles can be seen (H&E), indicating active B-cell proliferation and selection, exactly as in human. The overall compartmentalization with B cell follicular zones and T cell-rich interfollicular areas is conserved. In summary, the tree shrew tonsils exhibit the same tissue organization, epithelial characteristics, and lymphoid microarchitecture described in human and NHP tonsils.
RFigure 17: Histology of tree‑shrew tonsils (H&E). (A, H) Low-magnification transverse sections through the naso-/oropharyngeal region showing the pharyngeal tonsil in the nasopharyngeal roof and palatine tonsils in the lateral oropharynx; boxed areas indicate regions shown at higher magnification. (B–G) Higher-magnification views from panel A highlighting lymphoid follicles with germinal centers beneath specialized epithelia: stratified squamous crypt epithelium and ciliated respiratory epithelium overlying follicle-rich lymphoid tissue. (I–N) Higher-magnification views from panel H demonstrating additional micro-architectural features, including interfollicular zones, crypt structures, and epithelial specializations (e.g., ciliated mucosa and non-keratinized squamous epithelium) adjacent to follicles.
2. Protein‑level zoning (IHC). Marker localization recapitulates the canonical tonsillar micro‑architecture (RFigure 18). For example, T cells marked by CD3D are localized to the interfollicular T-cell zones and around crypts, whereas B cells (marked by CD79A, MS4A1/CD20, etc.) densely populate the follicles. This compartmentalized pattern of CD3+ T-cell zones adjacent to CD79A+ B-cell follicles is a hallmark of human tonsil histology. Furthermore, within germinal centers of tree shrew, we find the expected proliferation and germinal-center markers: many GC B cells are strongly MKI67 (Ki-67) positive, and express the transcription factor BCL6 in their nuclei, reflecting active centroblast proliferation and GC identity. The prevalence of Ki-67 high cells in tree shrew GCs (~80% of GC B cells) is on par with that in normal human tonsils. We also examined CR2 (CD21), a complement receptor highly expressed on follicular dendritic cells (FDCs) that form the stromal meshwork in GCs. In tree shrew GCs, CR2+ FDC networks are readily detected, outlining the GC structure – exactly as in human tonsils, where FDCs universally express CD21 in the light and dark zones14. We note that epithelial cell markers (e.g. pan-cytokeratins) in the tree shrew tonsil also showed expected patterns (highlighting the stratified squamous epithelium of palatine tonsil and ciliated respiratory epithelium of pharyngeal tonsil), further underscoring conserved tissue specialization. In summary, the spatial localization of immune cell subsets in the tree shrew tonsil (T cells, B cells, germinal center B cells, and FDCs) recapitulates the known histological organization of human tonsils, including the proper segregation of markers like CD3, CD20/CD79a, Ki-67, BCL6, and CD21.

Scale bars as indicated.
3. scRNA‑seq signatures: Single-cell data also show clear concordance of canonical tonsillar cell markers between tree shrews and humans. In the tree shrew palatine tonsil, we identified the expected immune cell subsets by hallmark genes – B cells (CD79A, MS4A1), plasma cells (JCHAIN, MZB1, XBP1), germinal-center B cells (BCL6, MKI67, AICDA), naïve/memory CD4+ T cells (LEF1, SELL, S100A4, TNFRSF18), Treg cells (FOXP3, LAG3), exhausted CD4+ T subset (CTLA4, TOX), CD8+ T/NK lymphocytes (CD8A, GNLY, NKG7), myeloid cells (CSF1R, CD68), and epithelial/secretory lineages (EPCAM, KRT14, AQP5, EPHA2). The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) contained parallel populations, including ciliated respiratory epithelial cells (TPPP3, NEK10), glandular cells (AQP5, FAM3D), goblet-like cells (KRT15, VMO1), and abundant lymphocytes (e.g. CD3D+ T cells, CD79A/CD19+ B cells, and JCHAIN+ plasma cells). These marker expression patterns are concordant with recent human tonsil single‑cell atlases (e.g., Massoni‑Badosa et al., Immunity 2024) that annotate the same compartments using these canonical genes15. We have added a brief statement in the Discussion noting the concordance of tonsillar architecture and canonical cell‑type markers between tree shrew and human tonsils, and we cautiously frame this as evidence of the tree shrew’s potential rather than superiority over traditional rodent models for studying pharyngeal lesions and respiratory‑acquired infections.
Changes in the manuscript: We have added a sentence description in the Discussion Line 396: “For example, our data show the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils of T. belangeri lie at mucosal interfaces directly exposed to the external environment and therefore constitute a first line of defence.. Together with the presence of well‑formed germinal centres and abundant lymphocytes which features not observed in rodent models48. These findings indicate similarity in immune landscape between T. belangeri and humans. Accordingly, T. belangeri shows promising application for studying pharyngeal lesions and respiratory‑acquired infectious diseases.”
2. A major caveat is that the EBV infection model does not mimic natural oral uptake and natural viral transmission which is observed in other NHP models with LCVs (i.e. rhesus and cynomolgus macaque models). Here, the route of EBV administration is intravenous into the femoral vein, thus any relevance to palantine/pharyngeal tonsil responses—which the authors argue is an important component of the tree shrew model (Fig. 2)—is unclear as this requires trafficking of the virus to the oral/throat cavity (in previous publications with this tree shrew model, EBV shedding occurs at 7 dpi). It is unclear why tonsil cells were not sequenced from the infected animals as this would highlight the importance and biological relevance of these structures for EBV infection. The I.V. infection route and also the high titer virus administered is akin to what is utilized in mouse models, which does not recapitulate natural EBV infection in humans and this needs to be acknowledged. As such, the immune responses (i.e. bypassing mucosal immunity in the oral cavity and gut that occurs with oral challenge) are expected to be skewed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment and agree that intravenous (i.v.) EBV challenge does not recapitulate natural oral transmission. We have clarified this limitation and our rationale as follows:
1. Study aim and rationale for i.v. infection. Our goal was to resolve early, spleen‑centered transcriptional dynamics of NR1H3⁺ tissue macrophages. To obtain a synchronous systemic exposure at defined early time points (3–7 dpi), we used a femoral‑vein inoculum. This minimizes the variability in uptake/kinetics inherent to oral challenge and enables detection of transient systemic programs with cellular resolution.
2. Explicit acknowledgement of route‑related limitations. We fully acknowledge that i.v. administration bypasses the oral mucosa and can skew early immune responses relative to natural infection by minimizing mucosal sensing. We now state this clearly in the Discussion and, in Methods, specify the inoculum strain, dose and route together with the rationale for using i.v. solely to synchronize early systemic exposure. Accordingly, our conclusions are restricted to early systemic (not mucosal) responses.
3. Why tonsils were profiled only at baseline. We profiled palatine and pharyngeal tonsils from uninfected animals to establish that tree shrews possess organized, human‑analogous tonsillar structures and to provide a reference atlas of their cellular composition (Fig. 2). These baseline datasets support the model’s suitability for future mucosal studies but are independent of the acute i.v.‑challenge cohort.
4. Why we did not sequence tonsils post‑infection here. The infection arm was designed around early acute time points (≤7 dpi) to interrogate immediate systemic responses in the spleen. Given this design, we did not power the study to capture oropharyngeal trafficking or early tonsillar events; therefore, we cannot draw conclusions about mucosal infection from these data. We now make this explicit in the manuscript.
5. Future directions: oral challenge and mucosal readouts. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added to the Discussion a dedicated paragraph outlining plans to establish an oral EBV challenge in tree shrews, with time‑resolved sampling of palatine/pharyngeal tonsils and paired throat‑swab virology, to directly compare mucosal and i.v. routes.
We are grateful for this constructive critique; the revision strengthens the framing and clearly delimits the scope of our conclusions.
Changes in the manuscript: We have added a sentence description in the Discussion Line 481: “Finally, because we used intravenous EBV inoculation to synchronize early systemic responses, our study does not model natural oral transmission or early tonsillar immunity. Mucosal innate and adaptive events may therefore differ from the responses reported here. Future work will establish an oral challenge in tree shrews with time‑resolved tonsillar profiling and shedding/transmission readouts to benchmark against the i.v. paradigm.”
3. The sample size for EBV experiments in Fig 4 is extremely small. Spleen cells are sequenced from only two animals that were infected with EBV and harvested at different time points, limiting the statistical power and generalizability of findings that NR1H3(LXRa+) macrophages are indeed altered by EBV infection. It is basically a pilot experiment. In an attempt to confirm scRNAseq findings, immunofluorescence and qRT-PCR experiments were performed on samples from 4 animals in Fig 4. No differences in NR1H3+ or IRF8+ macrophage numbers were detected by IFA, although the NR1H3 RNA level does decrease, which hardly confirms the scRNAseq findings. Given that data describing NR1H3 cell reprogramming is from n=1, additional evidence should be provided to support the major conclusions that NRH13+ macrophages dominate the inflammatory responses observed in EBV infection. For example, does depletion of these cells impact acute EBV infection? Are there additional signs of inflammatory markers that track with these macrophage subsets?
Response: We understand this concern. We agree that the original EBV arm in which one biological replicate per time point was profiled by scRNA‑seq was underpowered. In the revised study we have taken the following steps to strengthen the evidence and clarify our claims:
1. Increased animal numbers. We expanded cohort sizes to Control n=3, 3 dpi n=4, 7 dpi n=4 for scRNA‑seq, and to n=6/group for multiplex IFA and qRT‑PCR. The major biological patterns observed in the pilot dataset were reproduced including the early shift of NR1H3⁺ macrophages toward increased network centrality and inflammatory output, thereby addressing concerns about statistical power and generalizability (new Figure 4).
2. What we mean by “dominant” and why IFA counts do not change. Our conclusion does not hinge on numerical expansion of NR1H3⁺ macrophages. Consistent with the reviewer’s observation, IFA quantification shows stable numbers of NR1H3⁺ and IRF8⁺ macrophages across time points. Instead, the key finding is functional reprogramming: during acute infection, NR1H3⁺ macrophages become major signalling hub, with heightened incoming/outgoing communication strength. This is accompanied by loss of anti‑inflammatory programs in NR1H3_Macro (UCell score) while pro‑inflammatory programs in IRF8_Macro remain unchanged. Transcriptionally, NR1H3 itself decreases and TNF/IL1B/TNFSF and C1Q components increase in NR1H3_Macro. In the revision, we explicitly rephrase “dominates” as “emerges as a principal signalling hub and cytokine source during acute infection,” to avoid implying a change in cell abundance.
3. Depletion experiments. We agree that subset‑specific depletion in vivo would be definitive. At present, species‑specific depleting antibodies/conditional tools for tree shrew macrophage subsets are not available, precluding clean depletion without broad off‑target effects. We now state this constraint transparently and limit our claim to network‑level dominance and cytokine output rather than causal necessity in vivo. We also outline in the Discussion that future work will pursue targeted perturbations of the NR1H3 pathway once suitable in‑species tools are feasible.
4. Additional Functional evidence (human macrophage systems and ex vivo validation). To move beyond transcriptional associations, we added gain‑of‑function / pharmacologic tests showing that activating NR1H3 dampens inflammatory output: in THP‑1 macrophages, NR1H3 activation reduces IL‑1β, IL‑6, TNF‑α and diminishes effector polarization/IFN‑γ production of primary CD8⁺ T cells while leaving T‑cell proliferation unchanged; in primary human monocyte‑derived macrophages, the NR1H3 agonist T0901317 similarly suppresses LPS‑induced IL‑1β, TNF‑α, IL‑6 (RFigure 19, now compiled as Supplementary Fig. 18). These results are consistent with our model that down‑tuning NR1H3 removes a brake, enabling pro‑inflammatory output during EBV challenge.

Together, the expanded cohorts, clarified wording, and orthogonal functional evidence substantially strengthen the conclusion that NR1H3⁺ macrophages undergo early functional reprogramming and emerge as a principal signalling hub during acute EBV infection, even though their absolute numbers remain stable.

Response: We appreciate the pointer to the MHV68 study showing that loss of NR1H3 (LXRα) augments γ‑herpesvirus replication in mice, supporting a conserved immunoregulatory role for LXRα. Our work builds on and complements these findings in three ways.
1. We delineate a distinct NR1H3⁺ splenic macrophage subset with robust anti‑inflammatory/immunosuppressive features; this subset has not been explicitly delineated in mouse spleen datasets.
2. Mechanistically, we show that NR1H3 restrains the non‑canonical NF‑κB program: genetic and pharmacologic perturbations reduce NFKB2, MAP3K14 (NIK), NFKBIZ, and Cut&Tag reveals NR1H3 occupancy at/near regulatory regions of TNFSF14, NFKB2, NFKBIZ.
3. We provide cross‑species support, identifying a functionally analogous NR1H3⁺ subset in human spleen and showing by comparative single‑cell profiling that this program is readily detected in tree shrew and human, whereas it appears less prominent in mouse spleen, consistent with species‑specific cellular contexts rather than a lack of pathway conservation.
Together, these data refine how NR1H3 constrains inflammation via repression of non‑canonical NF‑κB in splenic macrophages and complement mouse studies by revealing a subset‑level, human‑relevant axis that is well captured in the tree‑shrew model.

5. The study largely focuses on describing B cells and macrophage subset, yet T cell responses are a major contributor to control of infectious agents that have been tested in tree shrew models (i.e. Zika, hepatitis virus). T cell populations should be described in detail.
Response: We thank the reviewer and agree that T cells are pivotal contributors to antiviral control in tree shrew models. While our study was primarily designed to resolve NR1H3⁺ macrophage programs under acute EBV challenge, we have now added a dedicated, lineage‑resolved analysis of splenic T cells (0/3/7 dpi) placed immediately before the cell–cell communication section (Supplementary Fig. S14). These new analyses revealed a robust IFN-γ (IFNG) induction in T cells and an enrichment of a CD8⁺ T cell subset expressing CXCL8, indicative of an active antiviral T cell response. We also observed significant upregulation of viral response pathways at 3 days post-infection (dpi), consistent with early immune activation against EBV (RFigure 20). These findings provide further context for the cell–cell communication results and underscore that T cells were engaged during early EBV infection. Given our macrophage‑centered objective, we did not pursue full T‑cell trajectory or TCR repertoire analyses here. We agree these will be informative, and we plan a follow‑up, EBV‑focused topic study to probe T‑cell dynamics in depth comparing oral vs i.v. challenge, sampling tonsil and other mucosal sites, and adding clonotype analyses across finer time points.
